en: (KauśS_1,1.1) Now we shall explain the ritual procedure. (KauśS_1,1.2) That, moreover, is based upon the sacred tradition. (KauśS_1,1.3) The sacred tradition, in turn, consists of both the mantras and the brāhmaṇas.
(KauśS_1,1.4) Just as the ritual procedure follows the Brāhmaṇa, so too do the mantras follow the characteristics of the ritual action;
(KauśS_1,1.5) likewise [there are those] with another purpose; (KauśS_1,1.6) and likewise the mantras follow the characteristics of the Brāhmaṇa.
In the absence of that, there is the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*),
because the Brāhmaṇas have been released [from their specific duties].
We shall now explain the sacrifice (*yajña*).
Facing east, he performs [the rite] for the gods and the ancestors in a low voice; wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder, he performs it for the gods.
(Wearing the sacred thread) over the right shoulder is for the ancestors;
(wearing it) over the left shoulder or facing northeast is for the gods; facing south is for the ancestors.
(KauśS 1.1.16) For the gods, [the ritual] ends toward the northeast; (KauśS 1.1.17) for the ancestors, it ends toward the southwest;
(KauśS 1.1.18) the rite for the ancestors is performed once.
(KauśS_1,1.19) At least three [verses] for the gods; (KauśS_1,1.20) or as prescribed;
(KauśS_1,1.21) moving clockwise is the practice of the gods.
(KauśS_1,1.22) Counter-clockwise for the ancestors;
(KauśS_1,1.23) the gods receive offerings with the utterance of *svāhā* and *vaṣaṭ*; (KauśS_1,1.24) the ancestors receive offerings with the utterance of *svadhā* and salutations.
The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for the ancestors is cut near the base; that for the gods is cut at the joints.
"Hand over the rib! (KauśS 12.3.31a).
Thus, he hands over a sickle for the purpose of gathering *darbha* grass.
Having cut above the joints with the formula, "May the plants be cut at the joint" (*oṣadhīr dāntu parvan*), and having brought it back silently, he places it to the north of the fire.
(KauśS 1.1.29) One should not turn away from the fire.
(KauśS 1.1.30) One should not pass between the components of the sacrifice.
(KauśS 1.1.31) Having extended the right knee, one offers the oblation.
(KauśS_1,1.32) That which is the earlier full moon is Anumati; that which is the later is Rākā.
(KauśS_1,1.33) That which is the earlier new moon is Sinīvālī; that which is the later is Kuhū.
(KauśS_1,1.34) Thinking, "Today is the fast-day," one who is about to fast eats food.
(Excluding honey, salt, meat,
and beans) (KauśS 1.1.36), having placed fuel sticks with the mantra "O Agni, may splendor be mine" (VS 5.3.1), he undertakes the vow.
"O Lord of Vows, [I enter] thee with the vow," or "the student, being under the vow,
shall sleep on the ground."

When the fire has been offered to in the morning, having washed his hands with the mantra, "For your work, for your dress, for your good deed" (*karmaṇe vāṃ veṣāya vāṃ sukṛtāya vām*), he spreads *darbha* grass to the west of the fire; upon that, he spreads a red bull-hide with its neck to the east and its hair upwards, and then prepares the two strainers (*pavitra*).
Having washed two *darbha* blades whose ends are uncut, he strokes them in the direction of the hair with the mantra:
"Purified by the mind of Viṣṇu, you two are pure" (*viṣṇor manasā pūte sthaḥ*). Then [he recites]:
"Thou shalt pass over the earth with might; thou sittest upon the altar, beautiful in the sacrifice. (*tvaṃ bhūmim aty eṣy ojasā tvaṃ vedyāṃ sīdasi cārur adhvare*) (*KauśS* 1.2.1).
The seers, bearing you as a purifier, do you cleanse us from our misdeeds.
Having placed the two strainers in between, he pours out the oblation with the formula:
"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I pour thee out, acceptable [to the deity]" (the full text—cf. 19.51.2, PS 5.40.1, TS 1.1.4.2, etc.).
Thus, with the formula "to Agni and Soma" (KauśS 1.2.2),
and with "to Indra and Agni" (KauśS 1.2.3), [one offers] on the new moon day.
(KauśS 1.2.4) The Āgneya [oblation] is always first.
(KauśS 1.2.5) Having poured it out, he sprinkles it with two purifiers [with the formula]:
"To such-and-such, thee, the beloved."

According to the respective deities, having washed the mortar and pestle and the winnowing basket, and having placed them upon a hide, he pours the rice grains into the mortar and threshes them; while doing so, he releases his speech three times with the call to the preparer of the oblation: "O preparer of the oblation, come hither! (AŚS 1.19.9, etc.).

Having husked them, made them well-dehusked, and washed the rice grains three times, he places the *caru* [oblation] upon [the fire] with the mantra: "O Agni, worthy of sacrifice, you have ascended from Varuṇa" (ŚB 11.1.1.6).
(With the words,) "Pure, purified," he pours water;
(with the words,) "Purified by the *brahman*."
Having thus [prepared] the rice grains,
he carries fire around them three times with the verse, "O Agni, we [place] a fortress around you" (RV 7.71.1).
(KauśS 1.2.11) He heats [the fuel] three times clockwise with a stirring-stick.
(KauśS 1.2.12) From this point onward, as he pleases.
(KauśS 1.2.13) He places the fuel on the north side of the fire.
The northern sacrificial grass (KauśS 1.2.15). [With the formula] "I sprinkle you, acceptable to Agni" (KS 1.10: 5.22), he sprinkles the fuel.
(KauśS_1,2.16) Having sprinkled a handful of *darbha* grass with the formula "(To the Earth)," (KauśS_1,2.17) he places it behind the fire with its tips pointing eastward, saying:
"Soft as wool, spread yourself out, a good seat for the gods. (cf. KS 1.11:6.2-3)
Having taken up darbha grass,
he places the seat of the Brahman priest to the south of the fire with the mantra: "Thou art the sacrificial strew of the seers."

Having spread [grass] to the east of the fire, covering the roots of some with the tips of others, he creeps around to the south of the fire as far as its western half, while giving the command: "Spread [the grass] around! (KauśS 1.2.20).
"By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, being impelled by his command, I strew around. Thus, performing an odd number of layers from the north,
he makes that place where they meet south-north.
One sprinkles that which has been spread [with the mantra]:
"I sprinkle thee, who art acceptable to the oblations.
That which is spread without being sprinkled shall not be fit for use.
(1,2.26) There is no kindling of fuel; (1,2.27) there is no oblation that has not been purified;
(1,2.28) there is no sacrificial implement that has not been sprinkled with water.
(KauśS 1.2.29) Upon that [hearth], he places the *sruva* ladle and the butter-pot, which have been washed and dried in the wind.

(KauśS 1.2.30–31) Having taken clarified butter that has been melted and strained, having placed it over the fire, having performed the *paryagni* rite, and having removed it from the fire toward the north, he sets it down behind the fire and purifies it with two strainers whose tips point northward.
(KauśS_1,2.32) "Thou art purified by the mind of Viṣṇu" (PS 20.45.7a).
(KauśS_1,2.33) "May the god Savitṛ purify thee from above" (PS 20.45.7b).
(KauśS_1,2.34) "With an unbroken filter, with a hundred-streamed, thousand-streamed, well-made [filter], I purify thee" (PS 20.45.7cd).
Thus the third [offering] (KauśS 1.2.35);
the fourth is performed silently (KauśS 1.2.36). He sprinkles the boiled oblation with clarified butter.

Having sprinkled [the oblation] with the mantra, "Anointing with honey, you shall act like ghee" (PS 5.16.3d), he removes it toward the north with the mantra, "We have prepared the cooked offering for Agni; sit upon the back, the abode of immortality" (PS 5.16.3ab). (KauśS 1.2.37)
Having placed the clarified butter behind and having adorned it, he purifies it with the same [formula];
he gazes at it with [the verse], "Not causing strife" (adārasṛt).
(The hymn beginning with) "Ut tiṣṭhata" (RV 7.72.1–3) is dedicated to Indra;
(the hymn beginning with) "Agnir bhūyām" (RV 12.1.19–21).
Thus he adds fuel with three verses:
"For him the lordships... (7.78.2) and "This kindling wood... (10.6.35). Or [he may do so] with these two.
(I yoke you with the divine *brahman* so that you may carry this oblation. [Note: The edition reads *voḍheva*, which is a misprint; cf. Zehnder 1999:
191. Manuscripts read *voḍhave*.]
"Like a carrier, O Jātavedas; kindling you, may we live long with good offspring and brave sons, bringing tribute to you. (MS 1.4.1:47.6 etc.
Having thus addressed it, he places a water-vessel filled with *jāṅgāyana* grass to the south and consecrates it. (KauśS 1.3.2)
"Likewise, hold the water-vessel just as Brahmaṇaspati,
whose nature is truth, held it in the beginning at the impulse of the god Savitṛ. (KauśS 1.3.3) Then he pours out the water.
Come here, O goddesses, clothed in immortality, golden-hued and of blameless form;
may the Waters, the Ocean, and King Varuṇa enjoy their shares of the oblation as they are poured together.
"Commanded by Indra, impelled by Varuṇa, may the waters carry up from the ocean to heaven. Commanded by Indra, impelled by Varuṇa, may they carry up the splendor from heaven to earth. (KauśS 1.3.4).
"O Jātavedas, I sprinkle thee around with Ṛta through Satya. (VaitS 7.4).

Having sprinkled water around [the fire] together with the oblations (*havis*) according to the rule [TB 2.1.11.1, etc.], and having sipped water and risen with the *jīvā* verses [ĀpŚS 19.69.1–4], he enters by means of the *vedaprapada* formulas: "Oṃ, I enter;
I enter *bhūḥ*; I enter *bhuvaḥ*; I enter *svaḥ*; I enter *janat*" [TA 4.42.2–4].

Having entered and having spread darbha grass behind the already-spread [grass], he gazes at the seat of the Brahman priest with the mantra: "O son of a remarried woman, stand aside from here; sit on the seat of another who is more foolish than we" (TS 3.2.4.4; VaitS 1.20).
"Cast out is the one who possesses wealth beyond [us], together with evil; cast out be he who hates us and whom we hate. With these words, he throws away a blade of grass to the south (cf.
139.38ff). Having touched that [grass], he mutters [the following].
Here I sit upon the seat of Arvāgvasu; I sit upon the seat of Ṛta; I sit upon the seat of Satya;
I sit upon the seat of the sacrifice performed; I sit upon the seat of the fulfillment; may the god not forget me.
—[ed. eva] Having sat down with the words, "The sacrificial grass is well-seated for you, soft as wool, free from sorrow" (cf.
AAśvSS 1.4.7) and "O most beautiful one" (12.1.29), he mutters the *brahmajapa* intended for the seat.
Bṛhaspati, as the Brahman priest, shall sit upon the seat of the Brahman.
O Bṛhaspati, protect the sacrifice.
[With the mantra: "That I may be able [to go] up from the heights and down from the depths" (TB 3.7.6.3), he wipes the *sruva* ladle with *darbha* grass [with the mantra:
"The *rakṣas* is burnt out; the enemies are burnt out. The *rakṣas* is scorched away; the enemies are scorched away" (TS 1.1.2.1). (KauśS 1.3.9)
Having heated it thus, he takes the *sruva* ladle by its base and mutters:
"Thou art the right hand of Viṣṇu, given by Pūṣan, [and] by Bṛhaspati;
thee, that *sruva*, the carrier of oblations for the gods, do I take" (*SāṅkhGS* 1.9.3).
"This *sruva*-ladle distributes the oblations with the *jagatī* meter consisting of a hundred syllables;
it anoints all the stations of the sacrifice. This is the Bārhaspatya offering, with divine protection. (ApSS 4.7.2).
Thus (KauśS 1.3.10): "Oṃ bhūḥ! For prosperity, I take you for well-being and for abundance."
Thus he takes the first draught;
"Oṃ bhuvaḥ! For prosperity, I take thee for prosperity"—thus the second.
(“Oṃ, heaven! I take thee for prosperity, for thousandfold nourishment,”) thus the third;
(KauśS_1,3.13) (“Oṃ, the world! I take thee for prosperity, for immeasurable nourishment.”)

Thus the fourth [verse] (KauśS 1.3.14), used in royal rites and rites of sorcery: "For the out-breath of so-and-so I take you; for the in-breath, the diffused breath, the level breath, and the up-breath..."
Thus the fifth [verse]:
"Agni in Agni, purified by the heart" (RV 4.39.9–10);
"Yoked in front" (RV 5.29.1).
He offers with the mantra, "The eye of the sacrifice" (*yajñasya cakṣuḥ*).

Behind the fire, in the middle part, he performs the offerings together; then, to the south of the fire, he pours the remnants of the clarified butter offerings into a water-vessel, prior to the eastern offerings.
The *purastāddhoma*, the *ājyabhāga*, the *saṃsthitahoma*, and the *samṛddhi* of the *śāntā* [mantras]—
these two are the *ājyabhāgas*. "To the bull, the great, the finder of heaven, to Agni, the radiant, I bring the bride-price."
May he not make us weak or powerless; may he grant that we live for a long time.
With the words, "To Agni, svāhā!
he offers the butter-portion for Agni in the northeast;
with the words, "To Soma," in the southeast. (KauśS 1.4.2)
O divine Soma, you who behold men, look along easy paths for us;
lead us toward our herd like one who knows the way, and come toward our yearning speech.
(With the formula: "To Soma, svāhā!
(KauśS 1.4.3), having spread a base of clarified butter in the middle of the oblation (KauśS 1.4.4), he cuts off the oblation twice with two joined fingers—from the middle and from the eastern half.
Having sprinkled the portion that has been cut off with clarified butter, he sprinkles the oblation twice;
from whichever part he cuts, he does so in successive order,
and thus for all the portions to be cut.

(Except for the *sauviṣṭakṛta* offering,) [one should perform] the first [offering], which is combined with the *purohoma*, [with the verse]: "Lead him upward" (*ud enam uttaraṃ naya*). (KauśS 1.4.8–9)
(KauśS 1.4.10) Thus he offers each preceding [verse] combined with the next.
(KauśS 1.4.11) The oblations are performed verse by verse, ending each with "svāhā.

(KauśS 1.4.12) That which he offers to the north of the butter-portion of Agni has the Rākṣasas as its deity; that which he offers to the south of the [butter-portion] of Soma has the Pitṛs as its deity.
Therefore, they should be offered in between; thus they are offered in the world of the gods.
That which one offers later after having first offered the former is "stepping away," and that sacrificer becomes worse off.
That which one offers subsequently in a continuous sequence is "stepping forward," and that sacrificer becomes more prosperous.

(KauśS_1,4.16) That which one offers where there is no fire is offered in the twilight; by that, the vision of the sacrificer is impaired, and thus the sacrificer becomes blind. (KauśS_1,4.17) That which one offers in the smoke is offered in darkness; thus the sacrificer becomes lusterless.
(KauśS_1,4.18) That which one offers in the light, by that he becomes endowed with spiritual splendor (*brahmavarcas*); therefore, one should offer in the light.
(KauśS 1.4.19) Thus, [with the mantra] "to him [Agni and Soma bestow] dominion" (RV 7.104.2), [he performs] the rite for Agni and Soma.
(KauśS 1.5.1) "O Agni and Soma, who possess common wealth and are invoked together, accept our songs! (RV 1.93.8)
You two became present among the gods.
O Agni and Soma, you two of one mind have placed these luminous realms in heaven;
O Agni and Soma, you released the rivers from the curse and from reproach when they were seized.
O Agni and Soma, whoever offers an oblation or presents a prepared sacrificial gift to you both,
he shall attain offspring, great heroism, and a full span of life.
O Indra and Agni, you adorn the luminous realms of heaven for the sake of spoils.
That heroic deed of yours has indeed been proclaimed.

(He) shall pierce Vṛtra and win booty—Indra and Agni, who are the two conquerors, whom one shall worship; they who rule over abundant wealth, most powerful through their might, and striving for victory.
(Indra and Agni, may they protect us— you two who are the progenitors of offspring—
may he, through that offspring, attain great heroism and a full span of life.)
(10.1.21cd + RV 1.93.3cd) O Indra and Agni, may we win that wealth which we implore from you— wealth consisting of cattle, gold, and horses.

At the new moon sacrifice, for the oblation to Indra and Agni, after the *svāhā* (utterance) [as prescribed in KauśS 1.5.3] and before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering [as prescribed in KauśS 1.5.4], there are the *pārvaṇahoma*s, the *samṛddhihoma*s, and the *kāmyahoma*s.
(KauśS_1,5.5) "Full behind" (at the full moon sacrifice);
(KauśS_1,5.6) "That portion which the gods prepared for you."
Thus, on the new moon day:
"To Ākūti, svāhā! To Kāma, svāhā! (KauśS 1.5.7).

For prosperity, thee, svāhā! For intention, thee, for desire, thee, for prosperity, thee, svāhā! [cf. TS 3.4.2.1 etc. Accomplish the hymn with the Ṛg-verse; accomplish the Rathantara with the Gāyatra.
Vast, following the path of the Gāyatrī.
[TS 3.1.10.1 etc. (svāhā) (KauśS 1,5.8) and with the *saṃnati* verses, beginning with "On the earth, for Agni, the pacification" [4.39.1–8].

And with the verse, "O Prajāpati, none other than you [RV 7.80.3]," having spread a base of clarified butter for all [the oblations] to the north, he takes a single portion from each and pours clarified butter over the two portions;
however, he does not do so for the sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*).
(KauśS_1,5.11) We have reached even the path of the gods, that which we were able to carry out;
may Agni, the wise one, perform the sacrifice—he indeed is the Hotṛ, he shall arrange the rites and the seasons.

Having offered the *avayuta* oblation in the northeastern quarter with the mantra, "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā! (as found in sakala PS 19.47.6 = ŚS 19.59.3, RV 10.2.3, etc.), he performs the *sarvaprāyaścittīya* oblations.
(Svāhā to those who are desired; svāhā to those who are undesired; vaṣaṭ to those who are undesired; svāhā! A healing medicine for the well-sacrificed, svāhā!)
Expiation for a bad sacrifice, svāhā!
For the divine bodies, svāhā!
(cf. BaudhŚS 1.21:32.10, HiraṇyakeśiŚS 2.6.1)
O Agni, you are *ayās* (unwearied) and free from reproach; indeed, you are the truth, you are *ayās*.
Created by an unwearied mind, being yourself unwearied, you have carried the oblation;
bestow healing medicine upon us.
"svāhā," he says.

(“Oṃ svāhā! Bhūḥ svāhā! Bhuvaḥ svāhā! Svaḥ svāhā! Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā! [KauśS 1.6.1] “O Jātavedas, whatever of mine has spilled from the mind, or whatever of the oblation has scattered wherever it may have been—the droplets and the spray—I offer them all together; may the desires of the sacrificer come true.”
"svāhā" (KauśS 1.6.2);
"that which of mine has been spilled" (VSK 2.5.3);
"that which through lack of mindfulness" (7.106[=111]).
And [the rites] for spilled [oblations] and for one who has forgotten [the formula] are the *skannāsmṛtihomas* (KauśS 1.6.3);
the *saṣthitahomas* are [performed with the verses] beginning "Whatever today as you set forth... (RV 7.97[=102].1–8).
With the verse "O Lord of the Mind" (*manasas pate*), he anoints the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with the final portion of the butter taken in four ladlings, using the remainder of the butter.
"For the earth, thee"— with these words [he touches] the root; "for the intermediate space, thee"— [with these words he touches the middle].
Thus for the middle; with "For the day thee," thus for the tip— likewise three times.
With the mantra, "The sacrificial grass is anointed" (KauśS 1.6.7), he offers the oblation according to the respective deity;
he holds the *sruva* ladle over the fire.
(KauśS_1,6.9) Whatever [remains] in the butter-vessel, that he pours out [with]:

"The powerful, great gods who partake of the poured-out remnants, who stand upon the sacrificial grass-bundle and sit upon the sacred grass—may all of them, praising this sacrifice, rejoice; Svāhā! May the immortal gods delight! [PS 20.35.2, TS 1.1.13.2–3].”
(Śrauta Sūtra 1.6.10) You are the *sruva* spoon, sharpened with ghee, the destroyer of rivals; sit in heaven!
Sit in the intermediate space! Sit on earth! May I become superior; may my rivals be inferior!
[As stated in *Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra* 2.4.2, etc. he places the *sruva* ladle with its handle pointing eastward (according to *Kauśika Sūtra* 1.6.11):
"By means of the sacred word (*brahman*), I release Jātavedas—the Agni who is the Hotṛ, the undecaying, who touches the chariot;
knowing all the births of the gods, may Agni carry the oblation according to their respective portions."
[He] places a fuel-stick [on the fire] with the words, "To Agni, svāhā! (KauśS 1,6.12), [reciting]: "Thou art fuel" (edho 'si). [7.89 (=94)]
[With the verse] "Thou art the second" (KauśS 1.6.13), [he offers] the second; [with the verse] "Thou art the fuel" (KauśS 1.6.13), the third; [and with the verse] "Thou art splendor" (KauśS 1.6.13).
(Thus, KauśS 1.6.14) he wipes his face; with his right hand, he strides three Viṣṇu-strides toward the fire (with the mantra:
"Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu," KauśS 10.5.25–27).
Thus he draws back the left foot with the right; saying, "The turning of the sun," he turns toward the right.
(KauśS 1.6.16) With the words, "We have gone to heaven," he gazes at the sun. (KauśS 1.6.17) "By the word of Indra, and of Mitra and Varuṇa..."
We shall raise up again the vessel established by Brahmā.
[—cf.
6.85.2ab, PS 19.6.2ab, AVPariś 37.19.2]—having carried around a vessel of water to the west of the fire, [he places it] to the north of the fire [with the verse]:
"O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss... [RV 10.9.1–5].
Having thus sprinkled [the water], he pours it into the joined palms of his wife upon the sacrificial grass with the mantra:
"I send you forth to the ocean" (TS 10.5.23–24).
With the mantra, "O people... (RV 1.32.1–4), or with the words, "May I become the wife of a hero," she wipes her face.
With the words, “The vows to the Lord of Vows,” he places a fuel-stick on the fire;
with the words, “Truth by means of the Real.”
Having thus sprinkled water around, he sets aside the remnants of the oblation toward the north (KauśS 1.6.21).
A full vessel is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) (KauśS 1.6.22).
One should not perform an oblation without a sacrificial fee; he who does so performs a malevolent spell against himself (cf. KS 37.12).
"Thus says the Brāhmaṇa (KauśS 1,6.23).
He feeds the Brāhmaṇas with the *anvāhārya* rice (KauśS 1,6.24).
Whatever in the sacrifice has been left unaccomplished, that is brought to completion by means of the *anvāhārya*."
(KauśS 1.6.25) This is the reason for the *anvāhārya* being called *anvāhārya*.
(KauśS 1.6.26) "Some gods are to be praised (*īḍya*), others are to be honored (*saparyeṇya*). The gods are to be praised; the Brahmins are to be honored."
(1,6.27) By means of the sacrifice itself, one gratifies those worthy of praise; by means of the *anvāhārya* (the guest-offering), those worthy of honor.
(1,6.28) "Both of these, being gratified, belong to him in the sacrifice" [cf.
KS 8.13:97.11ff]. (1,6.29) These two, the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), have been explained.
The *pākayajñas* are [included] within the *darśapūrṇamāsa*s.
One should perform the extraction from the very cooking-pot (*kumbhīpāka*) and offer it.

Having consecrated [the food] by means of placing it on the fire, carrying fire around it, sprinkling clarified butter over it, removing it from the fire, decorating it, and purifying it, [one should sacrifice].
(KauśS 1.6.34) Now there are also two verses:
"The ritual procedure prior to the *ājyabhāga* offerings, together with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering at the end,
and the oblations in the sacrifice, are the insertion (*āvāpa*), just as threads belong to a warp."
[Attributed to GB by Sāyaṇa I, p. 349] //

"Having performed the *pākayajñas*, one should perform them with a single portion of clarified butter (*ājya*), a single layer of sacrificial grass (*barhis*), and a single *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, even though the deities are different. (ĀśvGS 1.3.10).
By this, the New Moon sacrifice (*amāvāsya*) is explained. (KauśS 1.6.35).
In this case, the second [offering] belongs to Indra and Agni;
in the event of an inversion of these two, [one recites]:
"O Agni, you are the guardian of vows" (RV 8.11.1).

"Desires were at the beginning of that" (KauśS 1.7.1)— these [verses] are peaceful; in the absence of a specific instruction, one eats from the *sthālīpāka* (cooked rice in a pot) used in rites for prosperity, [the meat] being from a calf of the same color.
He offers clarified butter;
he places a fuel-stick upon the fire;
he scatters rice, barley, and sesame seeds.
(KauśS_1,7.6) He consumes the juices of milk-rice and sacrificial cake. (KauśS_1,7.7) He offers the stirred drink and the cooked rice.

(KauśS_1,7.12) From the rising of the sun;
(KauśS_1,7.13) the performance of the rites takes place in the forest to the east or to the north.

(KauśS_1,7.14) Having performed the rites at the northern edge of the water, having bathed with the hymns addressed to the waters (*apsu-sūkta*), having turned to the right, and having touched water, they return to the village without looking back.
The rinsing of the mouth, binding the hair, bathing, mounting a vehicle, and eating— these, when accompanied by the remnants of oblations (*saṃpāta*),
are all to be consecrated with mantras. Having bathed and sprinkled a woman who is ill, one wipes her, beginning from the head down to the tips of the feet.
Having first caused [the guest] to enter, he presents [the offering].
Having let curds and honey steep for three nights beginning with the thirteenth day, he ties [the mixture] up.
He causes [the guest] to eat.
(KauśS_1,7.21) While [the wife] holds on [to him], there are the consecrations and oblations;
(KauśS_1,7.22) behind the fire, on a hide, is the preparation of the sacrificial offerings;
(KauśS_1,7.23) a ball of bull-dung.
A skin from an animal killed while alive;
a stone without ears;
and he causes [the sacrificer] to sip water for the purposes of bathing and sprinkling.

(KauśS 1.7.27) He eats of those that have been brought together, or he anoints them. (KauśS 1.7.28) He causes the smoke of the fires to be directed [toward him]. (KauśS 1.7.29) The performance of the ritual act is with purity.

(KauśS_1,8.1) At night-rites accompanied by offerings made before the fire, in the forenoon, wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder, he sweeps the site of the hall; having eaten the food for the fast, bathed, and dressed in new clothes, he performs [the rites].
(KauśS_1,8.2) And at the rites for well-being, (KauśS_1,8.3) he carries the offerings to the quarters for those to whom sacrifice is due.
He worships each direction.
In every case, the ritual fee belongs to the performer.
There are three water-libations.
(KauśS_1,8.7) Those that follow are common and connected;
(KauśS_1,8.8) the peaceful collection (of materials);

(KauśS_1,9.8) Having released the waters with the words, "(atisṛṣṭo apāṃ vṛṣabhaḥ)," and having asked, "Are all these waters and plants [ready]? and being answered, "They are all," he should request permission, saying, "Oṃ, impelled by Bṛhaspati, may I perform [the rite]," and being authorized, saying, "Oṃ, impelled by Savitṛ, may you do so," he should proceed.
"One should perform [the rite] with the first [verse]," say Gārgya, Pārthaśravasa, Bhāgāli, Kāṅkāyana, Uparibabhrava, Kauśika, Jāṭikāyana, and Kaurupathi.
"One should perform it with either one," says Yuvā Kauśika; Yuvā Kauśika.
(KauśS 1 Colophon)
Thus ends the first chapter of the Kauśikasūtra in the Atharvaveda. (KauśS 2,1[10].1) Regarding the rites for generating intelligence in the preceding section:
(KauśS 2,1[10].2) one binds the tongues of parrots, mainas, and cranes.
He causes [them] to eat;
he places [fuel] consisting of Udumbara, Palāśa, and Karkandhu [wood];
he scatters [the grains].
He consumes [it];
he offers alms-food to his teacher;
he consecrates the ear of one who is asleep with a mantra.
(Sitting down,) he mutters [the mantra].
(Having offered) roasted grains mixed with clarified butter as a complete oblation,
and having offered those mixed with sesame seeds, he eats them.
Having placed a spotted staff to the east of the fire, he consecrates the parched grains on a black antelope skin to the west of the fire.
Having reached the end of the hymn, he hands [the staff] over;
he offers [the oblation] once.
He gives a staff and a deerskin. With the verse,
"I [am one] with the Rudras" (RV 4.30),

At the first utterance [of the child], he brings together the drops from the mother’s lap;
he feeds [the child] curd and honey;
and once [the child] has been initiated, he causes him to recite the ritual of a hundred-year duration.
He consumes it with the verses: "O Medhā, you are ours... and "...and may heaven for me... (KauśS 2,1[10].20).
He worships the sun with the verse,
"O Agni, what [you have] with heat... (RV 7.61),
and he consumes [the food] on the full moon day of Āgrahāyaṇī.
He worships Agni:
"In the morning, O Agni" (3.16);
"On the mountain, among the roaring crags" (6.69).
Having recited "divaspṛthivyāḥ" (6.125.2), he wipes his face;
these are the preparatory rites for the previous student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*).
(2.2.11.2) [The materials] beginning with the Audumbarī post;
(2.2.11.3) he places the under-layers from the student's dwelling;
(2.2.11.4) at the scattering of ants, he offers as oblation clarified butter mixed with fat, honey, Śyāmāka grains, and the tufts of *iṣīkā* grass.
Having poured the ants’ droppings into the remainder of the clarified butter, he goes to the village and offers them as entirely consumed oblations;
he gives food mixed with parched grain and sesame seeds to students of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*). These are the means for obtaining the village.
(2.2.8) Carvings from the base of the pillar for a modification, and coverings for assembly halls;
(2.2.9) food for the villagers;

From the left hand and heart, he eats blood mixed with essence.
*Pṛśnimantha* is the scraping from the tongue and the spreading and smearing over the eyes.
Having fastened the heart on a peg, he lets it soak for three nights in a cleansing solution;
he makes it into a powder,
pours it into a mash made of mixed grains, and eats it mixed with curds and honey.
(In this wealth) (yad ābadhnan) (the nine vital breaths).

Thus, having prepared a figure of a human body made of twelve *kṛṣṇala* weights of gold, perfumed with two pairs, and provided with the ritual residues (*saṃpāta*), he binds it; then, after twelve nights, he consumes it while not facing it.
(How is the *mahe* performed?)
Thus he eats rice cooked in milk with honey (*mādānaka*).

Having placed *vrīhi* and *yava* grains into the milk of a cow that has a calf of the same color as herself in a *camasa* bowl, having allowed it to thicken and having poured honey into it, he eats it.
He offers an oblation with the mantra: "To the Earth, to the Ear" (*pṛthivyai śrotrāya*).
"Vatso virājo" (The calf of Virāj)— these conclude with the *mantha* offerings;
"sahṛdayam" (with the heart).
*tad ū ṣu* [5.1.5], *saṃ jānīdhvam* [6.64],

May you be united; may your minds be united; may there be concord among us.
Thus, having carried around the village with the *sāṃmanasya* [offerings] containing the remnants of the water-oblation (*udakūlija*), he pours them out in the middle;
likewise for the *surākūlija*.
He causes her to eat the white, minced flesh of a three-year-old heifer; he prepares food, liquor, and a drinking-water station containing the *saṃpāta* residue.
For the first [offering],

(With) the three [verses] beginning with "audumbarī" (KauśS 2,3[12].12),
he consecrates the right thigh of the maiden;

He worships Agni:

With the verse, "From heaven and earth" (RV 6.125.2), he causes him to consume curd and honey;
for a Kṣatriya, that which is mixed with *kīlāla*, and for others, *kīlāla* alone.
With the mantra "The splendor of an elephant" (KauśS 2.4[13].1),
he ties on an elephant's tusk (KauśS 2.4[13].2).
Having smeared the body hairs with lac and having covered them with gold,
[one recites] "(In the lion,
in the tiger)" and "The glory is the oblation."
Thus, [there are] the hair from the belly of a Snātaka, a lion, a tiger, a goat, a black bull, and a king;

(KauśS 2.4[13].6) of these two...
In the morning, [one should worship] Agni on the mountain,
among the Aragārāṭas,
and between heaven and earth.
Thus, he eats the seven vital points mixed into the *sthālīpāka* offering (KauśS 2,4[13].7).

In this manner, having sprinkled unbaked vessels with *iṅguda* resin, he ignites them with grass using the *Āṅgirasa* fire;
those whom the smoke reaches, they conquer.

Having fastened a chariot-rim gem (*rathanemi-maṇi*)— encircled with iron, lead, bronze, silver, and copper, with a golden navel, scented, and bound with a thread— having placed it upon sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and poured oblations over it verse by verse, he recites the *bhṛṣṭis* with the two final verses of the *abhīvarta* hymn: (KauśS 2,7[16].30) "He has bellowed" (3.3), "Come to you" (3.4).

From where the clod was taken, thence are the ritual materials.
When the *puroḍāśa* has been consumed in the morning, they invoke the three [verses].

When about to consecrate the king, he prepares the water for pacification (*śāntyudaka*) at the Mahānadī from among those [plants] that have been specified, with [the verse]: "Be present among beings. (KauśS 2.8.1) (TS 4.8).
Having cooked a mess of boiled rice (*sthālīpāka*) and enclosed it on the south side, he sprinkles [the initiate] while he stands upon *darbha* grass.
He causes him to mount a bull-hide from a couch.
They both pour out a vessel of water.
While they are exchanging garments, the Brahman priest should say: "May our good deeds be together, and our evil deeds together. [The other should reply:
"Whoever shall do evil, let his evil be [his own]; may our good deeds be together."
He causes [the horse] to eat;

a village with a thousand [inhabitants] is the sacrificial fee.
The procedure up to the changing of garments has been explained by the [section on] the Sole King.
He sprinkles him upon the Darbha grass on the bed.

(KauśS_2,8[17].17) He sorts the prepared dice three times.

(KauśS_2,8[17].19) "I release it for the Brāhmaṇa; I release it for the Kṣatriya; I release it for the Vaiśya; let dharma be practiced in my district."
He proceeds;
he causes [the horse] to eat;
having mounted the horse, he leads it toward the Aparājitā [direction].
He goes to the assembly hall;

One approaches with products of the buffalo. Gārgya and Pārthaśravas say one should perform the rite for a cow; Bhāgali says no.

(KauśS 3.1[18].1) On each preceding full moon, at sunset on the edge of water, one clothed in black garments performs the rites dedicated to Nirṛti.
One should bury a *śāpeṭa* in a right-spiraling hole in a riverbank;
one sprinkles it with hymns addressed to the waters (*apām sūktaiḥ*);
one casts a black object into the waters.
Wearing new clothes and having fastened his sandals, he goes out toward the place where living beings are killed. Having stayed away, he performs the *sāṃpad* rite for that [place] in the north.
Having smeared a basket for cursing and bound it in water, he places a fire upon it and performs the *saṃpāta* rite.
He eats;
having placed [the food], he causes the black [dog] to depart.
Having tied on two worn-out sandals with his left hand and an old umbrella with his right, and having set fire to *śālā-tṛṇa* grass, he throws down a withered *vīriṇa* plant.
Having covered what was uncovered, he offers the oblation once;
he throws away his left shoe and his sandals; and having placed a withered *vīriṇa* grass mat upon it, [he performs the rite].
With the verse, "This is your womb" (RV 3.20), he pours grains mixed with gravel from an old granary;
with the verse, "Bring to us" (RV 5.7), he pours parched grains.

Together with two joined side-chests, he should place the third [chest] upon the left shank of a black bird; having bound the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) upon the side-chest, [the bird] should fly away from here [with the words]:
*pra patetaḥ*.
Thus he causes it to descend uncovered.

Having joined the blue [stripe], covered the red, and wrapped the white, he places the turban on his shoulder with the second [verse]; then, together with the left shoulder, he casts it downward into the water with the third [verse]—[the hair] being covered [with the first] and wrapped [with the fourth].
(3,1[18].19) For the former, the rite is the Citrā.

He places fuel-sticks anointed with ghee, each a span in length.
Behind the fire, on a line drawn upon the ground between two boats at a place of assembly, he eats the sweet liquid with his mouth.
He observes the *tejo-vrata* for three nights.
The consumption of that [offering] is performed with the verses "To Śambhu and Mayobhu" and "Brahma, being born."
Of this lovely one... (9.9);

With the verse, "They harness the ploughs" (KauśS 3,3[20].1), he stretches out the pair of the plough and the yoke;

"Come, Pūrṇaka!"— with these words [he addresses] the one on the north; [he addresses] the others as "plowmen."
"May the Aśvins prepare the plough; may Bṛhaspati protect it, so that there may be abundant grain, free from disease, and sufficient for many men.
With these words, he draws the plough over the field.
"Thou art possessed of food, O Dhārtarāṣṭra; may success attend me at thy sacrifice"—with these words he measures [the bricks].
"The foundations are struck down."
Having thus warded off [the obstacles] with cakes, he plows;
having reached the end of the hymn, he bestows [the gift].
They cause three furrows to run eastward, uttering auspicious words.
Having recited, "O furrow, we salute thee" (RV 3.17.8),
he sacrifices to Indra with a *puroḍāśa* cake at the northern end of the furrow,

They bring the remnants of the oblations to the furrow; having placed the northern portions of the *śaṣpa* and the sacrificial offerings into a water-vessel.
He anoints everything.
Wherever he pours the remnants, from there he takes a clod of earth; while she holds it, the wife asks, "Did you dig? and [he replies], "We have dug."
"What have you brought?
"Wealth, prosperity, nourishment, progeny, cattle, food, and the enjoyment of food.
Thus he scatters [the grains] to the north of the middle [line].
Having anointed the northern plowshare, he sets it aside for yoking in the morning.
Having spread *darbha* grass over the heads of the furrows, he places three cups each of *plakṣa* and *udumbara* wood:
those containing juice on the south, those containing young grass in the middle, and those containing sacrificial cakes on the north.
Having bent back the *darbha* grass-blades, he pours [the grain] together;
having placed balls of dung, *guggulu* resin, and salt into a cow with a calf of the same color, he eats them;
[he performs] the rite for the attainment of an ox.

They eat in the evening; they set aside the remainder until the next mealtime.
He consecrates it with the mantra,

and having sprinkled a stone upon the winnowing basket, he scatters and sows *kāśa* grass along with each verse.
With the mantra, "The cows have come" (*ā gāvaḥ*), he rises to meet the cows as they approach.
During the rainy season, he offers oblations three times with the first raindrop for Indra.
With the words, "May they be rich in offspring," he consecrates them as they set out.
[He does so] with a rope of twelve strands belonging to those who speak of the *karkī*, provided it has a *saṃpāta* [knot].
"This fodder... here is the calf" (KauśS 3,4[21].12)— this refers to what is stated in the mantra "That which is for your sorrow" (TS 5.1.3).
Thus, for the perfection of clothing (KauśS 3,4[21].13),
he places three spindles made of *kūdī* wood, wrapped in the nest of a spider and anointed with oil (KauśS 3,4[21].14),
which are further wrapped in reeds and a girdle of *mauñja* grass (as per Caland).
Having smeared it with honey and placed it upon the chickpeas (KauśS 3,4[21].15), [reciting:

In the same manner, on the full moon day, [he offers] those mixed with clarified butter.

Having stepped across and placed the fuel sticks, [he says]: "O you who are auspicious, possessed of offspring, and of good character, may I live as your householder."
Thus he grasps the pillar and worships it;
this is what is stated in the mantra: "That which I speak" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 12.1.58).
Having sat down upon the seat of the housewife, he pours out a vessel of water;
then, when about to depart on a journey, he looks at it, saying: "Stay right here! (RV 7.60.7).

(Satyam bṛhat [12.1])
Thus, on the full moon of Āgrahāyaṇī, behind the fire upon darbha grass in a pit, he eats a second portion that has been entirely offered and contains the remnants of the oblation.
On the third [occasion], he offers three times with seven verses beginning with "Aditi" and "O Mother Earth" (bhūme mātar).
To the west of the fire, having spread a cushion upon *darbha* grass,
he sits down with the verse, "O wide-spreading one... (*vimṛgvarīṃ*).
With the mantra, "Those of yours that are auspicious," he lies down; with the mantra, "That which while lying... he remains lying.

Thus, with the tenth verse,
"ud āyuṣā" (VS 3.31.10), he stands up.

(with the verse) "Rising up [12.1.28]."
Having thus gone out by the outer path toward the east or the north, he gazes [at the site] with the words, "As far as... and so forth.

(With the verse: "In which [the Sadas and Havirdhāna sheds are located]," he offers [thinking], "A bride will come to me.
(With the verse: "In which food [is found]."
Thus he approaches with the mantra,
"They bear a treasure" (KauśS 3.7[24].39), using this amulet for one who desires gold.
Having understood it thus,
he sips water from that which was prepared for the rainy season with the mantra "In which there is black" (*yasyāṃ kṛṣṇam*), and he applies it to his head.
"Thou whom the spotted mares on the chariot..."— here, the spotted mare is the sky and the red one is the sun;

(3,7.44) With the milk-rice of a spotted cow, an oblation offered entirely;

(KauśS 3 Colophon) Thus ends the third chapter in the Kauśika-sūtra of the Atharvaveda. (KauśS 4.1[25].1) Now, the medical prescriptions.
The medical treatment for a fever caused by a malevolent spirit.
(4.1.3) [He performs] the other [rite] according to the instruction.
(4.1.4) With the water-pot from the previous [rite], which is filled to overflowing, he anoints [the patient]. (4.1.5) He wipes away the wrinkles.

(2.3.1, etc.), he binds the tip of the *muñja* grass with a cord.

he blows upon him.
With the verse, "We know the arrow...
(KauśS 4.1[25].10), he ties on a urinary obstruction.
He makes [the patient] drink the dregs of fermented liquor that has been stirred with the excrement of a rat-hole and the remains of old *pramanda* liquor.
With the two final [verses], he causes [the child] to stand up,
makes him mount a vehicle,
and releases an arrow.
He unties the bladder;
he breaks the wick.
Having poured twenty-one barley grains into a milking vessel with water, and having propped up the udder at its base, he pours [the mixture] from the teat.
He causes him to drink a lukewarm decoction of *ālabīsa* for one suffering from upward-moving wind (*udāvartin*), and also for one suffering from upward-moving wind, with the verse:
"The mothers go... (RV 1.4.1).

It is explained by the removal [of the afflictions] through the *cātanā* rites. He places [stakes] made of *trapusa*, *musala*, *khadira*, and *tārṣṭāgha* wood;
[specifically] an odd number of stakes made of *khadira* wood.
With the mantra, "Pierce the two eyes" (*akṣyau ni vidhya*),
he drives them into the ground level with the earth behind the fire;
in this same manner, he does so for those made of iron and copper.

(KauśS_4,1[25].27) On the new moon night, having strewn around for a malevolent rite barley grains that have been taken once, not removed [from the husk], and ground without turning them back, he throws in fuel of *tārṣṭāgha* wood.
(KauśS_4,1[25].28) To whoever should come, he should say: "Scraping your tongue with a cord of hemp, leap out of the hall!"
Acting thus, while [the opponent] denies what is not his own, he offers *iṅguda* mixed with the down of *vīriṇa* grass into a hollowed leaf-cup;
he then hangs the sacrificial fuel and the sacrificial grass inside the hall.

Saying, "May I desire [this] for you" (*vāñcha me*) and "As this draft-animal [is yoked]" (*yathāyaṃ vāhaḥ*),

he touches together two trees and two creepers that have been touched; having mixed within the spaces between their bark-shavings the resin of *iṣusthaka*, *añjana*, *kuṣṭha*, *madugha*, and grass crushed with phlegm, he touches them while they are combined with clarified butter.
With the words, "Thou art a piercer" (*uttudas tvā*), he pushes it away with his finger.
He places twenty-one decorated, unspoken *prācīnakaṇṭaka* sticks.
(24) [He prepares] the edges of a small vessel together with threads. (25) Having smeared Kuṣṭha with fresh butter, he heats it three times a day for three nights.
(26) Having grasped a long blue lotus, he lies down.
Having tied the garment to three feet of hot water, (KauśS_4,11[35].27) [he should proceed]. (Ed.:
*prabaddhā*; Bloomfield, p. 358)
He lies pressing [the two testicles] with his two thumbs (the edition contains a misprint reading *ardayañ chate*;
see Caland, *Kl. Schr.*, p. 51).

(KauśS_4,11[35].28) He pierces the heart of the effigy with a scratching instrument made of *dārbhya* wood, smeared with *bhāṅga* oil, using a thorn-stake tipped with an owl’s feather and anointed with black lac.
(KauśS_4,12[36].1) With the mantra beginning "He of a thousand horns" (*sahasraśṛṅgo*), he performs the rite of inducing sleep.
Having sprinkled the hall with water from a vessel filled by drawing [from a well], he turns it upside down on the other side of the door-panel;
likewise for the naked one.
He addresses the mortar, the northern corner, the foot of the southern bed, and the threads with the following mantras.
(KauśS_4,12[36].5) With the verse, "The sky has stood firm" (RV 6.77.1 / 6.44.1), he performs the binding.
(KauśS_4,12[36].6) Having fastened the tip of the bamboo pole with a wrapping, he ties it to the middle finger.
(At the rite for) the foot of the bed, at the blue lotus,
at the drawn-in [thread],
and with the drawing-in [formula], he offers sesame seeds.
(KauśS_4,12[36].10) With the mantra, "This which is the beloved... (RV 6.89.1), he consecrates the head and ears;
(KauśS_4,12[36].11) he arranges the hair.
(With the verse: "May [the earth] with its cleft... (KauśS_4,12[36].12); (with: "The Nyastikā... (6.139.1); (and: "Here I dig... (7.38.1).
With the verse, "Thus [is] sauvarcala salt," he applies white flowers like those of a medicinal plant to his head and enters the village;
with the verse, "Of those won by chariots," he scatters beans and *smara* plants.
He hurls flaming arrows toward each of the directions, up to the *āvalekhanī* [the boundary-marking stone].

With the mantra, "Her fortune, her luster... (*bhagam asyā varca*), he buries a vessel made from the head of a woman who died in childbirth, or from the teeth-cleansing wood, or from the hair of one killed by *īśāna*, or from the skin of a sacrificial cow, into a mortar or a hole dug in a three-stone altar.
Having untied the garland, he recites [the formulas].
Having tied three circular tufts of hair with a black thread, [he places them] on a stone with three edges, one above the other, alternating their positions.
Then he digs out her *bhaga*.
"That fortune of yours which they buried at Triśila, and that at Catuḥśila—this I now dig up for you, together with offspring and wealth.
(KauśS 4.12[36].19) "I dig this [earth]. (3.18.1)
Having thus mixed the *bāṇāparṇī* with the juice of the red goat, he scatters it around the bed; then,
with the verse "I have placed [the fire] for you" (*abhi te 'dhām*),
he places a *palāśa* leaf underneath.
(With the verse,) "I have placed [the fuel] near you," he places it on top.
When about to lead away a person according to his desire, he goes along scattering innumerable pebbles with the *apāgha* formula.
Rubbing [the patient], he mutters;
not rubbing,
[he mutters] "(The flight of envy)" (Īrṣyāyā dhrājim).
"From the one belonging to all people" (RV 7.45.1) and "With the [spear] of Tvaṣṭṛ" (RV 7.74.3)—
these are the counter-recitations for the giving and the touching.
(With the first verse) regarding the ribs, as prescribed by the mantra:
"(Like the heat of) Agni" (RV 7.45.2),
he applies the axe-blade.
Having looked [at it] with the verse, "As one unstrings the bowstring... (RV 6.42.1), he takes up a stone;
with the second [verse], he places it down.
With the third [verse], he spits out;
in the shade, he makes it strung with a bow;
[this is the darbha grass].
Thus, like a medicinal herb (*oṣadhivat*), [one should recite] "O Agni, those born... (*agne jātān*);
[otherwise], one would not produce a hero (*vīra*).
Thinking, "May she not give birth to other living beings," one rubs the urine of a female mule with two pebbles against the food and ornaments,
and then gazes at the parting of her hair (*sīmanta*).
With the words, "Even cut down," he recites [the verse] for the wife regarding her lover;
at the place of the eunuch, he cuts down the obstructing bow.
He throws a stone into the water-pot with the verse,
"O Tṛṣṭikā... (VS 7.113.1), using the Bāṇāparṇī plant.
(With the mantra) "I take from thee" (*ā te dade*), he touches the items mentioned in the mantra; furthermore, he recites them one after another, and he recites them again.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Kauśika-sūtra of the Atharvaveda. (KauśS 5,1[37].1) "The mothers go" [1.4.1].

Thus are the knowledges of milk-rice (*kṣīraudana*), the *utkucastamba*, and the *pāṭa* (KauśS 5,1[37].2); the knowledge of the battle-altar (*sāṃgrāmikavedi*) (KauśS 5,1[37].3); and [the mantra] "Vena... (2.1.1).
Thus, he gazes upon five joints, a water-pot, a water-jar, a pillar, a pair of *kāmpīla* branches, fuel, dice, and twenty-one pebbles in his two hands.
Having wrapped the pot with a large cloth and placed it on a disfigured bed, he pours the remnants of the oblations over it.
Covering it so that no opening remains, whatever two maidens—possessors of stainless wealth—should carry it away from there, by that path the [lost object] is recovered.
In the same way,
when the plough has been yoked, he says to a young girl, "Take whichever clod you desire.
Among clods of various shapes and those from an anthill, the auspicious one is [the one she chooses].
"From a crossroads, she wanders much;
from a cemetery, she does not live long," he says,
pouring out a handful of water.
When she throws it toward the east, [he says] "Auspicious" (KauśS 5,2[38].1).
When they are approaching on a cloudy day, he rises up with the verse, "Born from the womb" (KauśS 1.12.1).
(5.2.2) Verse by verse, with water-thunderbolts;
(5.2.3) having taken up a flint-stick, a firebrand, and a cubit-measure;
(5.2.4) naked, rubbing his forehead.
Having cleared the ground outside, he offers *śigru* seeds and gravel upon a firebrand and a potsherd.
He establishes *kerā* and *arka* plants.
Having been surrounded by rain and ploughed in reverse order, he walks around three times and quickly scatters *arka* plants into the pit.
Having taken up a thunderbolt associated with the [mantras] "Homage be to you" (KauśS 5.2[38].8) and "That broad thunder of yours" (7.11.1).

(KauśS_5,2[38].9) For the first [rite], having wrapped together *soma*, darbha grass, hair, *iṣṭhānī* plant, *kuṣṭha* root, lac, *mañjiṣṭhā* dye, *badara* fruit, and turmeric with a splinter of birch bark, he buries it on top of the stirred drink (*mantha*) in the middle of a fertile field.
(KauśS_5,2[38].10) He eats curd with fresh [milk] until the conclusion of the rite.
(KauśS_5,2[38].11) These are the strengthening rites (*dṛṃhaṇa*), excluding the third [verse] of the *āśāpālīya* hymn.
(5.2.12) The rites for the earthen vessel;
(5.2.13) he places the sacrificial cakes upon stones within the corners; (5.2.14) both kinds are accompanied by the remnants of the oblations.
And in the case of assemblies and the distribution of shares, when there is no distress, one who is lying on one side of the abode of light mutters the *bhauma* [mantra]:
"This creeper... (RV 1.34.1).
Reciting, "Thus eating the *madugha*," he approaches the assembly from the *aparājita* direction; reciting, "May no enemy [be there]," he consumes the root of the *pāṭā* plant.
He recites;
he binds;
he wears a garland made of seven palāśa leaves.
(KauśS_5,2[38].22) With the mantra, "Those who eat...
(RV 2.35.1), he eats while observing a single meal in the assembly.
(KauśS_5,2[38].23) "The Brahman, being born... (RV 4.1.1).
Thus, when about to recite the chapters, he pronounces [the formula];
when about to consume [the food],
and when about to utter the theological debate (*brahmodya*).
While eating, he ties a loose rope with the mantra, "O Agni, may splendor be mine" (*mamāgne varcaḥ*); then he recites,
"And may the assembly be mine" (*sabhā ca mā*).
Thus he consumes;
he seizes the pillar and worships it with the verse:
"What I speak... (AVŚ 12.1.58).
Having recited the mantra as stated [in KauśS 5.2(38).30], "I am" (*aham asmi*),
he approaches the assembly from the Aparājita fire.
With the mantra, "Thou art a tearer, a tearer," he ties on a *srāktya* amulet;
to the east of the fire, he causes a reddish-brown cow to be brought forward.
To the west of the fire is a red goat for the sake of broth and meat;
those [substances] mentioned in the mantra [are required].
Having placed *vāśā*, *kāmpīla*, *sitīvāra*, and *sadaṃpuṣpa* [flowers],
[he recites]: "Thou art the destroyer of the destroyer" (*dūṣyā dūṣir asi*) and "Those who are in front" (*ye purastāt*).
"May you be the sovereign" (4.17.1);
"The light is equal" (4.18.1);
"And you are the one who makes no kinsman" (4.19.1).
"Suparṇas tvā" (5.14.1);
"yāṃ te cakruḥ" (5.31.1);
"ayaṃ pratisaraḥ" (8.5.1).
"Whatever they imagine"—
with these words he pours out the great pacification (*mahāśānti*);
having untied his turban at night, he proceeds while sprinkling water in front of him.

"To Yatā, to Yatā, to Śāntā, to Śāntivā, to Bhadrā, to Bhadrāvati, to Syonā, to Śagmā, to Śivā, to Sumaṅgali, to Prajāvati, to Suśīmā— O Vāmā, I have become yours," with these words he discards it from the absence [of the fire].
Beholding with a magical rite and an eye that sees enemies, [he looks] at the one who pierces.
"Thus, with the *kṛtyā*, he pierces the one who is arrogant" (KauśS 5,3[39].12); the "scraping instrument" has been mentioned (KauśS 5,3[39].13):
"O defiling one, thou art a defiler" (RV 2.11.1).
Thus, with a ladle, he sprinkles around the ankles three times with water that has been stirred together with the milk of a cow having a calf of the same color;
having poured broth and meat onto a wooden splinter, he causes [the patient] to eat it;
having bound the skin with sticks, the one who gives the command walks around and releases the bindings with a pair of tongs.
He causes her to lie down on her other side;
it is stated by means of a wooden splinter:
"Anointed" (KauśS 10.1.25).
Having bound it with a cord of *darbha* grass after reciting the mantra over fresh butter as prescribed,
[he should do so] while [the patient] is rising up.
Having thus raised [the vessel], he takes the lamp with his left hand and the water-pitcher with his right; remaining silent,
the one who issues the commands goes in front.
Unenclosed, not a place trodden by cattle, and not a pit dug for water.
He places it on ground sloping toward the south, or where it has split open naturally, or in a self-made hollow, or in a direction other than the usual;
having poured out a lamp from a gourd,
as [prescribed] for the sun.
Having turned back, he returns;
while standing, he loudly recites the *Mahāśānti* as it stands [in the text];
they sprinkle the vital points (*marmāṇi*).
He ploughs with a black plough.
Ten gifts are for the ploughmen.
The locations for malevolent rites are known from the mantras; these are the vital points (*marmāṇi*).
(With the verse: "When those [waters] flow together...
(RV 3.13.1), he proceeds while sprinkling water with whichever river he desires to enter;
he plants *kāśa*, *dividhuva*, *kava*, and *vetasa* reeds.
With the words, "This for you, O waters," he places gold upon it; with the words,
"This calf."
Having tied together a reed, a *añji* plant, a frog, and the two blue-and-red [threads] with a *kakṣa*-twig,
he covers [the site] with *avaka* grass while reciting, "Here, thus... (*ihettham*).
(At the place where it says, "Where this... [KauśS 3.13.7d]), he pours out [the water].

He offers three oblations to Varuṇa with a ladle made of *māruta* wood, using clarified butter from a *māruta* vessel, after having strewn the sacrificial grass with *māruta* grass and prepared a milk-rice offering (*kṣīraudana*) cooked over a fire of *māruta* wood.
The method of churning has been explained.
Having brought the curd-mash offering (*dadhi-mantha*) as a sacrificial gift (*bali*), he proceeds while sprinkling with the two *saṃprokṣaṇī* vessels;
having struck [the ground] with his hand or a cane, he sits down upon it.
With the mantra, "This is your womb" (RV 3.20.1), he deposits the fire into the two kindling woods,
or into his own self.
Descend, O Jātavedas! Once again, as a god among the gods, carry the oblation, knowing the way.
Rejoicing and exulting, endowed with brave sons, may we kindle you for hundreds of autumns.

With the verse, "O herb, may thy diggers be strong; thou art strong" (*yāṃ tvā gandharvo akhanad* ... *vṛṣaṇas te khanitāro vṛṣā tvam asy oṣadhe*), he causes it to descend. (*ŚāṅkhGS 5.1.7; KauśS 5,4[40].14*)

"You are a bull, O possessor of virility; we dig you for the bull," [with these words] he digs with an iron tool at the two swelling shoots that have been pierced through, while the bowstring is drawn over the two milk-mash mixtures placed in his lap.
The lap of Aditi;
cf. Bloomfield, SBE 42, p. 369, n. 2.
Having placed it, he drinks while sitting on a beam or a pestle,
as has been prescribed.
With the words, "Thus he ties the *arka* plant to the *ekārka* thread" (KauśS 5.4[40].17),
up to "to the body," he ties it to the black-skulled one with black hair.
"Be virile!"— with this, he approaches both; "Let them fly up together!"—
(with this).
One who desires rain should fast for twelve nights while reciting "pra nabhasva" (KauśS 5.5[41].2); observing all vows, he remains in a state of ritual exhaustion.
He sacrifices to the Maruts; as he offers to Varuṇa,
having caused the plants to be infused with the remnants, he turns them face down and causes them to overflow.
Having tied a dog’s head, a goat’s head, hair, and worn-out sandals to the tip of a bamboo pole, he makes them fight.

Having sprinkled [the opponent] with water from a vessel that has been filled by [the fighting], he places a stone on a three-legged stool made of *āmra* wood and sets it down in the water, [reciting]:
“This is your womb” (*ayaṃ te yoniḥ*).
One who is about to rise for the purpose of [reciting] "ā no bhara" (5.7.1) and "dhītī vā" (7.1.1) should place [the bricks].
He mutters [the mantra];
during the *pūrvā-aṣāḍhā* constellations he digs a pit; during the *uttarā-aṣāḍhā* constellations he piles it up.
Having spread out the gambling ground, [he recites]:
"The one who pierces through, the one who conquers" (AV 4.38.1);
"As the lightning [strikes] the tree" (AV 7.50.1).
With the verse, "This for Ugra" (*idam ugrāya*),
he scatters the marked dice;
[then he recites] "The mothers go" (*ambayo yanti*).
"May Śambhu be auspicious to us" (1.5, 1.6);
"The golden-hued ones" (1.33.1);
"That which is yonder" (3.13.1).
May they purify me.
(6.19.1) Those that have flowed forth...
(6.23.1) From the Himalayas they flow forth... (6.24.1)
"Purified by the wind with a strainer" (6.51.1);
"May there be well-being for us and joy for us" (6.57.3);
"To the oxen, you first... (6.59.1).
The verses "mahyam āpaḥ" (6.61.1) and "vaiśvānaro raśmibhiḥ" (6.62.1) are for the purposes of sprinkling and pouring water.
With the final [verse] containing the name of Vācaspati, he worships the rising sun.
Having bathed and put on unwashed garments, having washed himself, he puts on a washed garment and gives [a gift].

Following the instruction, "Just as meat... (KauśS 5.5[41].18), having caused the calf to run together [with the cow], having sprinkled it with cow urine, and having led it around three times, he applies the ointment.
He consecrates the horse's head and ears with the mantra "(The horse) swift as the wind" (RV 6.92.1);
when the horse has been bathed, he pours the remnants of the oblation over it.
(At KauśS 5.5[41].22) he causes [the person] to rinse with the powders of *palāśa* (at KauśS 5.5[41].23), and (at KauśS 5.5[41].24) he causes [him] to immerse [them].
He strews it with powders three times with the verse beginning "And with one" (RV 7.4.1),
and [he recites] "From the auspicious" (RV 7.8.1).
Having recited thus, when about to depart he should place [the fire];
he mutters [the mantra] and,
having sprinkled the vehicle with water, releases it.
He causes the substance, accompanied by the *saṃpāta* oblation, to rise;
having wiped it, he takes hold of it with the verse:
"Both of you have conquered" (*ubhā jigyathuḥ*).
Thus, with moist feet, [he performs] the act of conciliation (sāṃmanasya).
Having caused them to enter the village by means of a vehicle while facing westward, he gives [the gift]. Having returned and taken fuel-sticks—
Reciting "ūrjaṃ bibhrat" (7.60.1),
without forming a formal intention, he approaches and places [the fire] once,
reciting "ṛcaṃ sāma" (7.54.1).
With these words, he offers the Anupravacanīya oblation:
the third with the two [verses] beginning with *yuktā*,
and the fourth to Ānumati.
And this sacrifice is to be performed at both the *samāvartana* and the *samāpana*.
With the verse, "The celestial waters...
(*āpo divyā*), he who has completed his vow recites the mantra over the water for pacification at the edge of the water.
When the sun has set, having approached with fuel in his hand, he places the fuel sticks on the fire, omitting the third one.
He should then offer clarified butter as the oblation for the release of the vow (*vratavisarjana*) with the mantra: "For the year... (*idāvatsarāya*, PS 19.51.1–4).
One should place fuel sticks upon the fire:
"To the *idāvatsara*, the *parivatsara*, and the *saṃvatsara* year, we announce this:
whatever evil has entered into our vows, by that wickedness and impurity we are stained."
O Lord of Vows, whatever vow of mine the Day and Night have confused through error, may the Moon, rising in the east as a physician, set it right; may the Sun approve it with his rays.
Whatever vow I have transgressed through thought, mind, or heart—
may the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus kindle that for me.
I offer these vows to Agni, the Lord of Vows;
may he grant me great splendor, high renown, and long life.
Thus he establishes the concluding rites of the vow (*vratasamāpanī*).
For three nights he eats food without flavor; having bathed, he performs the vow.
[With the hymn] "Nirlakṣmyam" (RV 1.18.1).
With the words, "Thus he sprinkles the mouth of the one characterized by evil," he sprinkles [the head] verse by verse from the right side-lock of hair.
Having offered the *phalīkaraṇa* husks with a *palāśa* leaf, he pours the remainder back [into the vessel].
He places the *phalīkaraṇa* husks, chaff, and wood-shavings under the heel of his left foot.
He mutters the response while looking at the two [objects] with the *apanodana* and *apāgha* formulas;
he then ties on that which is prescribed by the mantra, beginning with "For long life" (*dīrghāyutvāya*).
(KauśS_5,7[43].1) With the verse, "Of Karśapha...
[3.9.1], he fumigates the reddish-brown cord, the staff of *aralu* wood, and whatever weapon there may be, with the chaff of grain.
(KauśS_5,7[43].2) He fumigates them with the husks of grain.
(With the verse:
"Beyond the deserts... (RV 7.41.1), there is the sacrifice performed while leading [the victim] beyond the dwellings at the end of the journey, as it proceeds along the path.
(KauśS 5.7[43].4) With [mantras] dedicated to Vāstoṣpati, he brings the sacrificial materials from the south of the fire onto ground ploughed by a plowshare.
(KauśS_5,7[43].5) He inserts the rites beginning with those for Vāstoṣpati into the Great Peace (mahāśānti).
(KauśS_5,7[43].6) In the central pit, he sows rice and barley upon *darbha* grass.
(KauśS_5,7[43].7) He sows the water for pacification, young grass, and gravel in the other [pits].
(At this very spot, the *dhruvā*— ) with these words, he consecrates the *dhruvā* ladle while it is being measured and raised;
having anointed it...
"By the *ṛta*"—this is what is stated in the mantra (*KauśS* 5.7[43].10).
"O woman, full... (*KauśS* 3.12.8).
Having thus taken up the water-pitcher and the fire, they enter;
he makes it firm with the two *dhruvā* verses and causes it to flow with the two *śambhūmayobhū* verses.
O Lord of the Dwelling, acknowledge us; be a gracious refuge for us and free from disease.
Whatever we entreat of you, favor that; bring here the four-footed and the two-footed creatures.
O Vāstoṣpati, free from disease, entering all forms,
be a most gracious friend to us.
With the verse, "Thus to Vāstoṣpati... (PS 20.23.2), he offers an oblation of milk-rice to Vāstoṣpati;
he feeds all kinds of food to the Brāhmaṇas and presents auspicious items.
(KauśS_5,7[43].16) With the words, "The fires which... and "The flesh-eater, unassailed," he ties on a *palāśa* leaf (KauśS_5,7[43].17) and offers an oblation.
He places [the grains] with a water-drawing vessel; having brought barley-grains with water into a water-pot, he performs the sprinkling with the verse: "Those fires... (KauśS 3.21.1).
Having stirred the mash with a ladle made of *pālāśa* wood, using two stirring-sticks made of *kāmpīla* wood, [he performs] the pacification rite with [the verse]:
"He who gives life... (RV 10.121.2).
Thus is the pacification of the barren cow (vaśāśamana).
He holds [the water] facing westward in front of the fire;
then, sitting behind the fire and facing eastward, while she [the woman] maintains contact with him, he prepares the water for peace (śāntyudaka).
There he applies this hymn;
with it he causes her to sip water and sprinkles her.
Standing [himself], while she stands, he recites the *mahāśānti* aloud.
Having offered with the mantra, "He who rules as the Lord of Cattle over cattle" (*ya īśe paśupatiḥ paśūnām*), he anoints the barren cow on the head, the hump, and the hindquarters;
he then anoints one edge of the sacrificial knife.
With an anointed [spoon], he digs out the omentum.
On the right side, he sprinkles it with two blades of *darbha* grass, saying, "For such-and-such [deity], thee, who art pleasing," according to the respective deity. (The verse:
"Out from the house... (KauśS 2.14.1).
Thus, with the firebrand, he carries it around three times counter-clockwise, not carrying it around himself;
[the sacrificer] takes hold of it with two *darbha* blades.
Behind and to the north of the fire, he thrusts it in, with its head toward the west and its feet toward the north.
"Be united with her body," he says, and thus he causes one blade of *darbha* grass to settle [upon her];
then he establishes the vital breaths.
Standing to the south, while reciting "Knowing... (KauśS 5.8[44].16), he mutters the *rakṣohan* formula (KauśS 5.8[44].17);
when the animal has been immolated, he offers the oblation.
If a barren cow has bellowed out of lack of ritual action, or if she has struck with her feet,
may Agni release me from that sin and from all distress.
Having approached with a water-pot [as prescribed in ManB 2.2.8 etc.], the wife, having gone toward him, washes her limbs beginning with the face, [saying]:
"O face, be purified for the service of the gods. (KauśS 5.8[44].18–19)
"Vital breaths," [he says] regarding the two nostrils;
"sight," regarding the two eyes;
"hearing," regarding the two ears.
(With the mantra: "Whatever is cruel in thee, whatever is fixed," he sprinkles all around the cord-foundation.
(With the mantra: "The tracks," having gathered them from the footprints.
"The navel" means the navel;
"the penis" means the penis; "the anus" means the anus.
