"O Heaven and Earth, grant us fearlessness," and "Thou art a hawk,"— with these words, one who desires fearlessness should offer oblations to the Seven Seers in each of the directions.
To the north, the giving of the staff to one who has been initiated or to a religious student takes place;
with the verse "And heaven and earth for me" (RV 6.53.1), he offers it to Heaven and Earth.
(KauśS_7,10[59].29) With the mantra beginning "He who is in the fire" (RV 7.87.1), one who desires well-being should [offer] to the Rudras, desiring well-being.
(KauśS 7 Colophon)

Thus ends the seventh chapter of the Kauśika-sūtra of the Atharvaveda. One who is about to establish the sacred fires, or one who is about to offer sacrifices, kindles the *brahmaudana* fire for a year,
or for a day and a night.
Or one may act according to one's desire;
however, a year-long [observance] is recommended.
For that purpose, there are either the *sava*-fire and the *senāgni*-fire, or they are produced by churning.
For both are recognized as the *aupāsana* fires.
In that [fire], one should offer clarified butter with the *devaheḍana* formula; one should also place fuel-sticks upon it.
Or he gives pieces of wood;
upon that [fire], he offers oblations according to his desire— one, two, or all of them—
or else he causes the giver of each individual blessing to recite it for himself.
(8.1.12) The recitation of blessings follows; (8.1.13) and [it applies] to those blessings that are not specifically designated.
(8.1.14) The two givers perform the rites; he recites the mantras over them according to their respective characteristics.
With mantras having both genders, he addresses both; with those in the masculine gender, the giver; and with those in the feminine gender, the wife.
This is done excluding the command for the water-carrier.
Now, the sacrificial ground.

Now, that which is level, with its roots intact, unburnt, firmly established, sloping toward the northeast—having strewn it with clods of earth from a mound, with *darbha* grass, and with the hair of animals, he consecrates them while they are being churned, reciting: "O Agni, be born! (KauśS 11.1.1).
The wife adapts the mantra,
and the sacrificer does as well.
(KauśS_8,1[60].22) “Produce smoke,” for smoke; (KauśS_8,1[60].23) “O Agni, you have been born,” for what has been born; (KauśS_8,1[60].24) “Kindled, O Agni,” for the kindled fire.
Having recited "Thus being kindled" (KauśS 8,1.25) and "Go forth,
O woman" (11.1.13), he gives the command regarding her while she is well-guarded and adorned.
With the mantra, "Come hither" (KauśS 8.1[60].26), he consecrates her as she approaches; with the mantra,
"Arise, O woman" (KauśS 8.1[60].27).
Having thus given the command to his wife,
he receives [the vessel] with the words: "Take hold of the jar" (ŚS 11.1.14d).
"Thou art the portion of strength," with these words he places it down;
"This great earth... with these words [he places it].
With the words, "Thus he spreads the skin, with the neck to the east and the hair upwards" (KauśS 8.1[60].31),
he spreads the skin; with the words, "A man mounts a man" (ŚB 12.3.1), he causes him to mount the skin.
The wife calls out;
on the third occasion, she calls after the offspring,
as instructed by the seers.
With the verse, "Thus," he places the water-pot upon the hide;
with the verse, "The waters are sons," the two women, accompanied by their offspring, descend after him.
(With the mantra) "Towards the east, towards the east," as stated in the mantra,
they go around four times with a water-vessel.
Facing each direction,
they pay homage with the mantra: "This is the firm Virāj."
Having descended to the ground with the words, "Like a father his sons," they perform the water-related rites with that [water] and sprinkle themselves with purifiers (*pavitra*).
(8.2.6) With the tips of two *darbha* blades, he sprinkles the animal sacrifice (*carma-havis*).
(8.2.7) He hands over the designated portions to the woman who has given birth (*sāñjanatī*).
(8.2.8) Those [portions] are divided into three parts.
Having said this, he places the rice in the bowls.
Of those [portions], he performs the *śrāddha* with that which belongs to the ancestors;
he feeds the Brahmins with that which belongs to humans.

With the mantra, "O Agni, he who among the gods... (RV 10.53.4), having bent his right knee, facing the Aparājita direction, or bowing low, he pours [the grain] into the pot with handfuls, open palms, and joined hands.
With the verse, "Either from the pot, or four... and "Those seven sacrificial essences," the two [parents], together with their offspring, touch [the child].
"I take your hand" (KauśS 8.2[61].14) refers to what is stated in the mantra; "three suitors" (KauśS 8.2[61].15) refers to KauśS 11.1.10c.
"Choose three boons," [he says];
with this ritual act, he chooses "the firm ones" as the first boon;
those which are the other two, they are the wife.
(These two pressing-stones [11.1.9]) _(This pressing-stone [12.3.14]) _,
having placed the mortar and pestle and the washed winnowing-basket upon the hide, [he sets them down].
"Take hold of the two pressing-stones," with these words he takes hold of both;
"Together with kinsmen."
With the words, "Thus he pours the rice-grains into the mortar" (KauśS 8.2), he pours the rice-grains into the mortar;
with the words, "The Lord of the Forest" (VS 12.3.15),
he raises the pestle.
"Having crushed the stalks, [he removes] the seizing evil"— with these words he threshes.
With the words, "This is thy thought" and "Increased by rain," he takes up the winnowing basket.
"May offspring [arise] upwards," and "O all-pervading one"— thus they carry her upward.
"Clean it away!
and "The husks, the chaff!"— thus she who is winnowing.
"Various forms," thus [he says] to her as she is pouring out;
"the three worlds," [thus he says].
Having touched them while reciting, "Thus, may they not be exhausted" (*KauśS* 8,2[61].28),
he pours them out with the verse, "May they come back again to the winnowing basket" (*ŚB* 12.3.20d).
"Upaśvasa," he says, fanning it; "Pṛthivīṃ tvā pṛthivyām," [he recites].
Thus he smears the pot;
"O Agni, the porridge," with these words he places it on the fire.
"Agni is the cooker," with these words he places the final fuel stick around; "Instructed by the Ṛṣis."
Thus he draws away the water:
"Pure, purified" (Śuddhāḥ pūtāḥ), "purified by means of purifiers" (Pūtāḥ pavitraiḥ).
Having placed the two strainers in between with the words "Thus," he pours water [with the mantra]:
"Purified by the Brahman" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.1.18).
"Measured, small" (KauśS 8.2[61].37)—
having washed the rice grains in those waters, he pours them out with the mantra "Be wide, spread out" (KauśS 11.1.19).
He says, "They stir up" (*ud yodhanti*), "he cooks" (*śrapayati*),
and "give the axe" (*pra yacha parśum*);
thus he gives the sickle for the gathering of *darbha* grass.
"May the plants cut me at the joint," with these words he cuts above the joints;
"fresh sacrificial grass."
Thus he spreads the sacrificial grass (*barhis*): "Arise for the altar" (*udehi vedim*), "Supporter, support yourself" (*dhartā dhriyasva*).
With the words, "Thus he causes it to be removed" (KauśS 8.2),
and with the verse, "Turn back to us," he turns the cooking pot clockwise.
With the mantra, "O Lord of the Forest, [upon] the strewn [grass]," he places the vessel upon the sacrificial grass;
[he places] the shoulder-supporting [vessel] with the mantra, "The shoulder-supporting."
He places [the brick] with the formula, "Thus he places" (KauśS 8,2[61].45),
and spreads [an underlayer] with clarified butter with the formula, "Spread [the underlayer]" (ŚB 12.3.2.7).
With the mantra "upastarīḥ," he consecrates that which has been spread out;
with "aditer hastān," [he takes from] her hands.
Having taken water from there, he pours it into a vessel, as prescribed by the mantra "sarvān samāgā" (KauśS 8,3[62].2).
With a ladle, from the cooking pot,
he pours back into that very same [vessel] what was made with the ladle;
having taken the uppermost portion with the ladle, a friend, sitting to the south of the fire facing north, holds it.
Then he draws it out.
Once it has been drawn out, whatever he holds having set it aside, that he places upon the northern half.
For the sake of avoiding the state of being neither upper nor lower, that which is the upper part of the rice is the "upper" [portion]; the rice itself is indeed the rice.
(KauśS_8,3[62].9) With the words, "In the sixth autumn," he places it behind the fire.
(KauśS_8,3[62].10) [With the verse: "O guardian of treasure, [guard] the treasure."
Thus he makes three sections;
this is what was stated in the mantra beginning with "Whatever [the wife]... (Yajurveda 12.3.39).
She takes hold of her husband; while they are holding on, he performs the rites from this point forward: "The two fires, the Rakṣases... (KauśS 12.3.43).
"Thus he carries fire around [the victim]" (KauśS 8,3[62].15);
[he recites] "O Adhvaryu, of the tawny one" (11.1.31) and "I have reached this" (12.3.45).
Thus he performs the *upari-āpāna* (the drinking from above).
He should say, "O Brahman, [drink] from the brown one," provided that he is not the *adhvaryu*.
With the words, "The limbs with clarified butter" and "Pour the ghee," he causes it to flow with clarified butter.
With the verses, "The streams of wealth" (VS 12.3.41) and "To the Ādityas and Aṅgirases" (VS 12.3.44),
he sprinkles with the juices.
(“The beloved of the beloveds,”) with these words, he consecrates the milch-cow and the other items to the north of the fire.
(He addresses) her [with]: “She has moved forward as the first” (PS 5.31.1).
Having caused [the cow] to be milked as prescribed, he sprinkles [the milk] with the verse:

"The first one, about to be milked, has approached, bearing all sacrifices, belonging to all the gods. She lets her calf loose; the lowing cow bellows. She has been released; being well-disposed, she makes the sound *hiṃ*."
Bind the calf, place it [at the udder], and enjoy; having cleansed yourself, O milker of cows, sit down and milk.
Swelling with nourishment, pour out for him the rice-porridge, the sweet drink, the clarified butter, the exhilarating draught—the portion of food.
"May she, well-milking and with her calf, run along the first path here, given by Yama the King.
Given not hurriedly, she has come here first; unite the cow of all forms with her calf. (PS 5.31.1–3) (KauśS 8,3[62].22).
"This is my light" (11.1.28).
With the verse, "The fires together" (RV 12.3.50),
he places gold upon it; with the verse,
"This is the skin of the cows" (RV 12.3.51).
With the verse, "Thus [is] Amā," he places a garment together with gold in front;
with the verse, "That which is in the dice," they both wear the same garment.
That second [portion] becomes a garment for the wicked; some say one should give it to a blind man.
With the verse, "The oblation cooked for thee" (RV 10.87.1), the one who knows the *Bhṛgu-Aṅgiras* lineages places the four *ārṣeya* priests [in their positions].
(“Pure, purified,” as stated in the mantra;
“cooked from the field.”)
"Rain down!"—with these words he removes the husks into the fire. (KauśS 8,4[63].6) [cf. ŚB 11.1.29]
With the words, "Thus he scatters the husks" (KauśS 8,4[63].7), and with the words, "The outer [parts] are the kernels" (ŚB 11.1.29b), he sweeps away the chaff with his left foot.
"Thy body is the heavenly world"— with these words he scatters the other [grains].
"O Agni, go forward"— [with this verse].
One should offer clarified butter with the mantra "samācinuṣva" (VS 11.1.36);
this is the consecration for the *savas*.
Those [mantras] whose purpose has been fulfilled are set aside;
he adapts the mantra according to the specific requirement.
He should examine the characteristic mark immediately following the mark of that which has been worn, in accordance with the sequence of the ritual actions.
Alternatively, by means of the characteristic mark (*liṅga*),
the sequence of the arising of the ritual action is praised;
because it does not arise otherwise, [the order] follows the characteristic mark.
There is either a combination of those with equal purpose or an option between them.
Now, the distinction between these two:
first, he makes it possessed of *saṃpāta* by means of a *sūkta*.
Having consecrated it with the hymn beginning with "śrāmyataḥ" (KauśS 8.4[63].20) and having recited it aloud, the giver, while being addressed, should give it;
he makes the subsequent portion accompanied by the *saṃpāta* oblation using the *anuvāka*.
Having consecrated [the offerings] with the section beginning with "To the eastern quarter thee" (KauśS 12.3.55) and having addressed them, the giver, while being spoken to, should offer them;
or he may offer them separately according to their respective deities— this is the basic rule.

(8.4.24) All [the rites] are performed according to their origin, with the exception of the five *odana* offerings for the teachers. (8.4.25) Furthermore, there is no repetition of those [rites] already performed. (8.4.26) Some [prescribe] a cow together with gold as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
The Kaurupathi should give a cow as the sacrificial fee;
having consecrated it with the *saṃpāta* formulas and addressed it, the giver, being exhorted, should present it [with the words]:
"This is the portion. (KauśS 8.4[63].27–29) (etaṃ bhāgaṃ [6.122.1])_
The *saṃsthita-homas* (concluding oblations) are performed with the verses beginning "etaṃ sadhasthāḥ" (6.123.1) and "ulūkhale" (10.9.26).
He scatters [the seeds] and performs the consecration with the mantra:
"Of the quarters... (KauśS 8.5.1).
Thus, with the verse beginning "The four bowls" (KauśS 8.5[64].2) and "When kings... (3.29.1), he gazes [at the offering].
For one who has bathed his feet, he places cakes on each of the feet;
a fifth on the navel.
While being lifted up with a garment, [the vessel] containing gold and the remnants of the oblation [is placed upon him].
(“Bring this one,”) with these words he consecrates the goat being led from the unconquered region;
(then he recites: “For Indra, the portion.”
With the verse, "Thus, as the fire is being led around" (KauśS 8,5[64].8), and with the verse, "Those who hate us... (ŚB 9.5.2c), as it is being consecrated.
(With the mantra: "Pra pado," while he is washing his feet; (with the mantra: "Anuchya śyāmena."
With the verse,
"Thus entering limb by limb," he [addresses] the one who is placing the pot on the fire.
"Pour it out," he says as he pours;
"Lay it down," he says.
When they say,
"Thus laying down" (KauśS 8,5[64].14), [the officiant] says, "Lay it around completely," as they lay it around completely.
"Let the cooked [offering] go," [he says] as he removes it;
"Step forth from these two," [he says].
Thus, [he addresses] the one who is lifting [the goat] onto the *darbha* grass behind the fire:
"I anoint the lifted [goat]" (*uddhṛtam ajam anajmi*).
"With '... thus he anoints it with clarified butter' (KauśS 8,5[64].18), and with 'the fivefold rice-offering' (4.14.7)," as stated in the mantra.
He places the portions of boiled rice separately on the [four] feet; he places the fifth in the middle;
having sprinkled the southern rear portion with the sacrificial post.
(With the mantra: "The goat is cooked," he [takes] its skin with the head and feet attached, [reciting: "For the goat...
With this hymn, as prescribed,
he places the "upper garment" (*uttarā-mota*) containing the *saṃpāta* oblations before it, together with gold.
(Five gold plates...)
Thus it is stated in the mantra (KauśS 8.5[64].26).
To the north [are placed] the cow and other items, along with a cushioned covering, a garment, and gold (KauśS 8.5[64].27).
"Bring this one" (ĀpŚS 9.5.1).

With this hymn, [the rite] ending with the application of collyrium is performed while collecting the remnants of the oblations; it is explained by the five-oblation rite of the hundred-porridge [offering],
beginning with the verse "Of those who intend evil" (RV 10.9.1).
In this case, he addresses the mouth that is being bound with the mantra:
“The thunderbolt among rivals” (10.9.1b) and “This one is indeed the pressing-stone” (10.9.2d).
He spreads it with the mantra as prescribed, "The altar is thine," while it is falling.

In twenty vessels for mixing rice, they place one hundred portions of meat bound with leather straps, each upon a separate portion of rice. In the first perforated vessel among those in the middle row, they place curdled milk (*āmikṣā*); on both sides of the tenth, they arrange seven cakes each;
and in the fifteenth, two sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*).
Gold at the front;
water-jars with the verse "O divine waters" (*apo devīḥ*) at the head.
With the hymn beginning "Bālās te" (KauśS 8.6.9),
having led her three times clockwise around the fire while she holds the *sampāta* mixture, the procedures for seating, washing the feet, and sipping water have been described.

Having poured water into his hand, he then takes two portions from the middle of that rice-oblation and from its eastern half; having sprinkled them with water from above, he offers them [with the verse]:
"Purified by Soma, sit in the belly of the Brahmins. (KauśS 8.6[65].11–12)
"O Odana, I place you among the seers" (KauśS 8.6[65].13).
Then he eats it (KauśS 8.6[65].14):
"I eat you with the mouth of Agni, with the mouth of Bṛhaspati."

"I place you in the belly of Indra, in the stomach of Varuṇa, so that he may consume it as an offering and a sacrifice. The divine self consumes you; you are my self; do not harm my self within my self.
With these words, he consecrates what has been consumed.
The fire named Nṛmaṇas, which has entered among the Brāhmaṇas—may this well-offered rice-oblation be for him; may he not harm me in the highest heaven.
"May he be for us in the highest heaven" (PS 20.57.15;
cf. PS 16.72.9)—with these words, he causes the giver to recite.
The procedure up to the inspection of the *śataudanā* is explained by the morning recitation (*prātarjapa*).
He consecrates those things mentioned in the mantra with the words, “May speech be in my mouth” (KauśS 8.7[66].1), and with the verse,
“The mind with the Bṛhat” (KauśS 8.7[66].2).
He responds with the mantras: "And may heaven be mine" (6.53.1) and "May my vital power return to me" (7.67.1).
When the mantra has been recited over it, they eat after having divided [the food].
At the Śataudana rite, there are one hundred and twelve sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*);
for one who gives more than that, his gift becomes a fulfiller of desires.
With the mantra, “He is the Brahman of this,” he makes pools in the rice porridge in each direction;
above is the drinking-place.
On both sides of that, there are four channels belonging to the directions;
he fills them with juices.
Having placed upon the earth, in each direction, those things mentioned in the mantra, such as *āṇḍīka* and so forth, along with wine and water.
"The rice porridge which..."—
thus [it is] beyond death; "the ox..."— [thus it is].
With the mantra "Thus the ox" (KauśS 8.7.13) and "The rays of the sun" (RV 4.38.5), he gives a white cow as the *anūbandhyā* sacrifice.
With the verses, "This spotted cow" (RV 6.31.1) and "This one,
a thousandfold" (RV 7.22.1),
[he addresses] the spotted cow.
"O gods, this barley mixed with sweetness... (KauśS 8.7[66].15)—with these words, he offers the *paunaḥśila* oblation, which is sweet, accompanied by gold, and provided with the *saṃpāta* residue.
"May the divine folk purify me... (KauśS 8.7[66].16).
With the verse, "Thus the purifier, the kṛśara" (KauśS 8.7), [he offers] the kṛśara;
with the verse, "Who [knew] the speckled one?
(RV 7.104.1), [he offers] the urvarā.
(With the verse beginning) "A thousandfold" (*sāhasra*),
he [addresses] the bull;
(with the verse beginning) "And Prajāpati" (*prajāpatiś ca*).
"Thus [he gives] the ox" (KauśS 8.7[66].20);
"Homage to thee as thou art being born" [10.10.1];

Having sprinkled the cow with water from a vessel containing the remnants of the oblation, having consecrated it with a mantra, and having addressed her, the giver should present her while being made to recite: "The earth receives you" (TS 3.2.9.8).
Thus he accepts her.
Regarding the phrase "upamitām" (the measured): that which is to be given together with rice is placed inside and covered;
however, that which is declared by a mantra is praised.
"Of thee that is sacrificed to, I unfasten," with these words he opens the door; "Thee, facing westward, I, facing westward... with these words [he enters].

Having thus taken a water-pot and fire, they enter. He performs the *saṃpāta* rite within that very place with the hymn (*sūkta*). Having sprinkled the hall with the water-pot containing the *saṃpāta*, having consecrated it, and having pronounced the formula, he should give [the gift] while the donor is being addressed.
(8.7.28) “Between heaven and earth,” with these words he receives her; (8.7.29) “the one who has been brought near.
Having consecrated it with the mantra beginning with *iti mantroktāni pracarati* and *mā naḥ pāśam*, he holds it.
(“His bones,” as it has been stated;
“having gathered all of this together.”)
Having thus poured water into a pit and scattered [the materials], he offers the *śataudanā* (hundred-meal oblation).
When the *sāvika* ritual materials have been gathered together, he chooses a Brāhmaṇa as the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*).

(8.8) [One should give] to a seer (*ṛṣi*), a descendant of seers (*ārṣeya*), one who possesses excellent sacrificial fees (*sudhātudakṣiṇa*), and one who is not subject to external causes (*anaimittika*).

(8.8) Indeed, he is a seer, a descendant of seers, and one who possesses excellent sacrificial fees, whose ancestors for three generations back are known to be endowed with learning, conduct, behavior, and virtue.
(8.8) Some say [this applies] during the northern course of the sun (*udagayana*).
Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the preparatory rites of the *odanasavas*.
Having performed the *savas*, one should establish the sacred fires;
some say this applies to all Vedic schools.
All the Vedas are of two types.
The consecration (*dīkṣā*) lasts for at most one month, or twelve nights;
some say it is three nights.
They should eat sacrificial food and observe celibacy;
they should sleep on the ground.
The performer and the donor should not eat at will until the completion [of the rite], provided that the rites are continuous.
Some say that [the rite] is completed on the day [of the full moon].
For the sake of the journey, the two donors—or the donor alone—should have their hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved;
the wife, however, should shave herself except for her hair.
Having bathed, wearing unwashed garments, being fragrant, observing the vows, and being fit for the ritual, the two fast.

On the following day, having put on the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*), having prepared the water for peace (*śāntyudaka*) and sprinkled the sacrificial site (*yajñavāstu*), and having churned the *brahmaudanika* fire, [he recites]: "Whatever offense against the gods...
(*yad devā devaheḍanam*).
While the giver has taken hold [of the vessel], one should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* with these three hymns: *yad vidvāṃso yad avidvāṃsaḥ* (6.115.1) and *apamityam apratīttam* (6.117.1).

In the forenoon, having kindled fuel from a *śānta* tree outside [the village] facing east, having swept around it, sprinkled water, and spread the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), having set down a vessel of water and performed the ritual service with clarified butter,
and having offered the regular preliminary oblations (*purastāddhoma*) and the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*).
To the west of the fire, having spread out a red hide of a bull or an ox with its neck to the east and the hair facing upward,
he prepares two strainers (*pavitra*).
He takes two blades of *darbha* grass with unbroken tips, washes them, and strokes them in the direction of the grain.

(Bending) the right knee, facing the *aparājita* direction, or bowing low, with a fist, an open hand, or a hollowed palm—with whichever vessel he intends to cook [the rice]—he takes a fourth portion with that [vessel], and four portions with a shallow bowl (*śarāva*), [saying]: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ... [PS 16.70.1].
(From TS 2.4.6.1, etc. "To the seers, to the descendants of seers, to the one-seer, I offer you who are pleasing.
(KauśS 8.9[68].1) "May the Vasus offer you with the Gāyatrī metre; may I enjoy inexhaustible, undecaying strength. (Cf. PS 16.70.2+3)
Thus he causes the giver to recite:
"May the Rudras [protect] you with the Triṣṭubh metre;
may the Ādityas [protect] you with the Jagatī metre."
"May all the gods, with the *anuṣṭubh* metre, set thee apart!
May I live upon inexhaustible, undecaying nourishment!"— with these words he causes the giver to recite.
(KauśS_8,9[68].3) He touches the offered oblation with the hymn.
(KauśS_8,9[68].4) The *svarga* and *brahmaudana* rites share the same ritual framework (*tantra*).
(KauśS_8,9[68].5) At their conjunction, one should pour this much water into the *brahmaudana*, divided into two portions.
(8.9.6) As many grains of rice as there may be, one should not pour water over them, nor sprinkle water upon them.
(8.9.7) If one should pour water over them, [one should recite:

"The good protector" (RV 7.6.3),
and "The great one, indeed" (RV 7.6.2).
With these words, he causes him to board a boat containing gold and barley, [reciting]: "The stone-bearing river flows" (RV 10.53.8), and "Arise, cross over, O friends! (RV 10.53.9).
With the words "Thus he delivers the northern [direction]," [he offers] pebbles and so forth until the placing of the fuel-stick;
from the verse beginning with "Vaivasvata" onwards, it is the same.
Having reached the house, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is performed in common.
Now follows the Piṇḍapitṛyajña:
it is known to take place on the new moon day (amāvāsyā), in the evening, at the time when the sun has set during the day.
With the mantra, "May Mitra and Varuṇa encompass me" (KauśS 11.8.3), he washes his hands; with the mantra,
"Me with splendor" (KauśS 11.8.4).

Having sipped water thus, he again performs the *apasavya* rite by sipping with his left hand and gives the instruction to the one who issues the calls: "Wash the mortar, the pestle, the winnowing basket, the sacrificial pot, and the bronze vessel; bring the sacrificial grass and the water-pitcher."

Wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder, facing the intermediate direction between the south and the east, he pours out the sacrificial grains for the oblation upon a winnowing basket covered with a single strainer, saying:
"This for Agni Kavyavāhana;
Svadhā to the Fathers who dwell on the earth."
Thus, this [is the formula]:
"Svadhā to Soma accompanied by the ancestors" (Pāṇini 18.4.72),
and "to the ancestors who possess Soma" (Pāṇini 18.4.73).
"To the fathers who dwell in the intermediate space" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.259),
and "to Yama, accompanied by the fathers" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.260).
With the mantra, "Svadhā to the ancestors who dwell in heaven," he pours out three oblations toward the south;
having placed them in the mortar, he threshes them three times.
"O fathers, this is your oblation," [he says];
as is the oblation, so he attends to it,
for the Pitṛyajña is indeed the oblation itself.

They instruct the one who has performed the *praiṣa* (the call): "Wash the *caru*, place it on the fire, pour water into it, and cast in the rice grains; stay there stirring with the stirring-stick (*mekṣaṇa*), and do not seize the head.
They declare that seizing the head is a fault.
Having gone out by the outer door, wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), he faces the intermediate direction between the south and the east.
With the words "Let them rise up" (*ud īratām*),
he digs a trench one span deep, one finger-breadth wide, and one finger-breadth long;
according to some, it is one joint-breadth deep.
"Struck down are the Asuras and Rakṣasas who sit among the Pitṛs"— with these words, he sweeps up the dust toward the south-east;
then, having washed both his hands and the trench.
"O fathers, this is your vessel," [saying this], he fills the trench with water,
pours in the whey or fresh butter by means of a ladle, and moves it out toward the south.
Taking two pieces of wood,
he sets them on fire with the verse beginning, "uśantas... (RV 10.16.4).
(One) replaces one of the two that are aflame;
having taken away one with the verse, "Be right here, a winner of wealth" (RV 18.4.38).
Having placed them in the dust, he adds fuel to them with the verses:
"Those which were buried" (VS 18.2.34) and "They kindle together" (VS 18.4.41).
With the verses "Those who have thirsted" (KauśS 18.3.47) and "Those who are true" (KauśS 18.3.48),
he places the ritual materials together. (KauśS 11.8[87].23)

(The items required are: water for sprinkling, sacrificial grass (*barhis*), a water-jar, a bronze vessel, a ladle, clarified butter, a stirring-stick, the cooked rice-offering (*caru*), garments, collyrium, and ointment.

Having gathered whatever else is to be brought together here, he—being now wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*) and then over the right shoulder for the ancestors (*pitryupavītī*)—takes the sacrificial grass, unties the binding cord, and lays it down toward the southwest, the eighth direction.
Having sprinkled the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with water, [reciting]:
"The fathers who sit upon the sacrificial grass" and "The fathers have been invited by us."
The Agniṣvātta ancestors;
those who are our father’s fathers; those who are ours.
Thus he spreads [the grass];
[he performs] the three [rites] beginning with the summoning (*āyāpana*),
[starting with] *ud īratām*.
With these three verses, he should pour out the water-pots one by one according to the verse;
thereafter, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder for the ancestral rite (*pitryupavītī*), [he recites]:
"Those Dasyus... (VS 18.2.28).
Having thus carried a firebrand blazing at both ends three times from right to left, he throws it away; having sprinkled water around [the fire], [he recites]:
"Those who, assuming various forms, being Asuras, move about with their own inherent power..."
"O Agni, drive them far away; may the blessings of our ancestors be true for us! Svāhā! Svadhā! Having offered thus, he pours clarified butter over the *kumbhīpāka* (the cooked mess).
He offers with the mantra, "To Agni Kavyavāhana" (VS 18.4.71). He offers the second oblation according to what has been set aside, with the mantra,
"To Yama Pitṛmat" (VS 18.4.74).
"svadhā pitṛbhyaḥ" (VS 18.4.78)— this is the third [verse] (KauśS 11.9); "yad vo agniḥ" (VS 18.4.64).
Having thus sprinkled water around the rice grains with the *sāyavana* formula and the rice grains together with *darbha* grass with the verse "saṃ barhiḥ" (VS 7.98.1), [he proceeds].

Therefore, wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī) and wearing it over the right shoulder for the ancestors (pitryupavītī), he draws up [the food] with the ladle (darvī), [saying]: "The sky is the ladle—undecaying, unlimited, and unfailing. Just as that sky is the ladle—undecaying, unlimited, and unfailing—even so is this ladle of the great-grandfather undecaying, unlimited, and unfailing."

The intermediate space is an inexhaustible, immeasurable, unfailing ladle; as the intermediate space is an inexhaustible, immeasurable, unfailing ladle, so is this ladle of the great-grandfather inexhaustible, immeasurable, and unfailing.
(KauśS_11,9[88].10) The earth is an inexhaustible, immeasurable, unfailing ladle; as the earth is an inexhaustible, immeasurable, unfailing ladle, so is this [ladle].
"Thine is this ladle, inexhaustible, unlimited, unfailing"—having thus lifted it up and mixed it with clarified butter, he places three compact balls [of food], saying:
"This for thee, O great-grandfather. (KauśS 11.9[88].11) [Śrautakośa I, Eng. I, p. 488] (cf. ŚB 18.4.75).
To the south, for the wives:
"This for you, O wives.
This [is for] women and men who have made aspirations, who are currently aspiring, and whose [hair] is scattered or disheveled.
"May there be inexhaustible *svadhā* for all those to whom we are givers and who depend upon us, together with their wives"—
saying this, he scatters rice three times in a counter-clockwise direction.
Having scattered tufts of grass and collyrium into clarified butter,
he deposits them while reciting, "Come hither, O Fathers! (addhvam pitaraḥ).
"Grow, O fathers; do not separate yourselves from us further than this, O fathers"—with these words he applies the threads. "They anoint, they anoint apart. (ŚB 18.3.18)
Thus, with the formula for anointing (*abhyañjana*), he continuously pours clarified butter (*ājya*) over the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*s) with the mantra:
"And those who are living... (*ye ca jīvā*).
"Those who have gone away before" (KauśS 11.9[88].18), and "O fathers, rejoice here; according to your portions, according to your worlds, rain down [blessings]" (cf.
VSM 2.31, ManB 2.3.6, etc.).
"Here, O wives, rejoice; according to your portions, according to your stations, be fertile!"—
having thus looked toward the fire that is within the fires from left to right, he faints three times.
Having turned back, [he recites]:
"The fathers have rejoiced; according to their portion, according to their world, they have been satisfied. (KauśS_11,9[88].21)

"Those wives have rejoiced; according to their portion, according to their world, they have been sprinkled with rain. Thus [he says], "The waters [have sprinkled] Agni. (KauśS 11.9[88].22–23) (ĀpŚS 18.4.40)
Having thus sprinkled the fire with water, [he recites]:
"Satisfying the son and the grandson... (KauśS 11.9[88].24).
Thus.
"May my great-grandfathers, grandfathers, and fathers, together with their wives, be satisfied; may they sip water.
Having sprinkled [water] counter-clockwise, [he says]:
"O my great-grandfathers, grant me heroes; O my grandfathers, grant me heroes; O my fathers, grant me heroes."
He prays to the heroic ancestors (KauśS 11.9[88].26) and worships them with the mantra: "Homage to you, O fathers" (ŚB 18.4.81ff.).
Having shaken the northern *sica* with the mantra, "They have eaten" (*akṣan*), he recites, "Go away" (*parā yāta*).
Thus he causes [the food] to go away.
Thereafter, wearing the *yajñopavīta* for the ancestors—that is, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder—he says: "That mind which was not here with the ancestors, that I summon hither."
Thus he invokes the mind:
"We invoke the mind with the Nārāśaṃsa hymn, with the praise-song,
and with the prayers of the ancestors."
May our mind return to us again for the sake of will, for strength, and for life, so that we may long behold the sun.
May our fathers and the divine folk grant us back our mind; may we be united with the company of the living.
O Soma, may we, bearing our minds within our bodies, abide in your service, possessed of progeny.

"May the prosperity of those living beings who are born together with me, who are well-disposed, and who belong to me among all living beings, be ordained for me in this cow-pen for a hundred years. [VSM 19.46, etc. Thus.
Whatever remains of the cooked rice in the *carusthālī* vessel, one should consume it while it is still warm; then one should give it to a Brāhmaṇa.
If a Brāhmaṇa cannot be found, one should cast it into the water.
According to some, one may give it to a trusted servant.
He gives the middle *piṇḍa* to his wife who desires a son, [saying]:
"O Fathers, bestow a fetus, a boy adorned with a lotus-wreath,
so that there may be a man here."
"May the dappled bull, the foremost, mount you; O Fathers, you have placed the wise one as a germ.
May this man come to you, a man from among men; may he be born for your preeminence; may he sing the *sāman* at the Soma sacrifice. (cf. RV 9.83.3) Thus [it is said]. (VSM 2.33, etc.)
If there is another second wife, [he gives] something else to her;
[he gives] the most excellent portion to a learned Brahmin (*śrotriya*).
Now, if his wife or a female slave becomes a runaway, he gives to her those rice grains which have been scattered counter-clockwise.
"Come hither; do not turn away.
Food is the bond of breath; with that I bind you to me."
Having taken the water for sprinkling and the fuel sticks with the verse, "Mā pra gāma... (ŚāṅkhGS 13.1.59), [he proceeds] according to the ritual for ancestral offerings (KauśS 11.10).
Having returned thus,
he worships the house with the verse, "Bearing strength... (RV 7.60.1).
"Rejoice, do not fear; you who dwell in this cow-pen with your manure-heaps, yielding strength, pure, and observers of pure vows—may we, as living beings, sit down among you in our homes."
The gods have granted me strength, and men have granted me strength;
from the ancestors I have brought strength. Full of strength be my home.
The gods have given me milk, and men have given me milk;
from the ancestors I have brought milk; full of milk are my homes.
"O gods, you have given me vigor; so too have humans.
From the fathers I have brought vigor; my home is full of heroes. Having recited this, he places the fuel-sticks into the fire while remaining inside.
"This Agni is our overseer; he is the best finder of wealth for us. By sitting near him, may we not suffer harm; may he protect our progeny."
In this house of our own, may a thousand prospering fires flourish;
may we kindle this fire together, long-lived and full of splendor.
"O Agni, you who are praised" (RV 18.3.42);
"O Agni, may we kindle you" (RV 18.4.88)—thus (KauśS 11.10[89].14); "He has become the messenger" (RV 18.4.65).
With these words, he brings back the fire (KauśS 11.10.15).
If the entire fire has been carried forward (*praṇīta*), then this is for one who maintains the *āhitāgni* fires;
however, even in the domestic (*gṛhya*) rite, it is for one who does not maintain the *āhitāgni* fires (the edition reads *gṛhyeṣv*).

"Whatever has been done by me, may I be able to accomplish that; may the ancestors indeed know me"—thus [he says]. (cf. Caland, *Ahnencult*, p. 15) (KauśS 11,10[89].17) (idaṃ cin me kṛtam astīdaṃ cic chaknavāni / pitaraś cin mā vedan [-])_iti.
The gods know him who sacrifices; men know him who gives; the ancestors know him who performs the *śrāddha* rites—the ancestors know him.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter of the *Kauśika-sūtra* in the *Atharvaveda*.
Intending to have the honey-mixture (madhuparka) brought, he causes darbha grass to be brought; then he has mats (viṣṭara) prepared:
the first, for the water for washing the feet, consists of a single branch; that for the seat consists of two branches; and that for the honey-mixture consists of three branches.

Having taken as many [stalks] as he deems necessary, having separated and prepared them—both the roots and the tips—so that they may be as wide as possible, he draws them upward and binds them together at the middle with the formula:
"By *ṛta* thee, by truth thee, by austerity thee, by ritual action thee. Thus he binds them.
Then he releases [the arrow] with the words: "Released is the hater who hates us and whom we hate.
And with the words, "And of this giver," he looks at the giver.
Then he causes water to be brought, saying, "Water for the feet, sir. Having consecrated it with the verses beginning "Golden-hued," he first draws forward his right foot, saying,
"May I maintain within myself sacred knowledge and ascetic fervor."
When the right foot has been washed, he draws the left one forward with the words,
"May I maintain both the ruling power and the common people.
He then consecrates the two washed feet with the following mantra.
"May these two feet, washed with water, endow the Brahmin with glory; may the waters used for washing the feet burn away my enemy.
(AitB 8.27) [KauśS 12.1(90).12] He looks at the giver, saying, "And of this giver... [referring to the giver].
Then he causes a seat to be brought,
saying, "A seat with a grass mat, sir.
He sits upon it facing westward.
Having placed his feet upon the seat with this verse, "The earth, which is rich in grass," he says:
"He who hates us and whom we hate is overcome."

And [the priest] looks at the giver, saying, "Of this giver. Then he causes water to be brought, saying, "The guest-offering, sir! He responds to that with the mantra: (KauśS_12,1[90].16) "Of this giver," thus he gazes at the giver.
(KauśS_12,1[90].17) Then he causes water to be brought, saying, "The *arghya*, sir! (KauśS_12,1[90].18) He addresses that with the following mantra.
You are the mouth of foods; may I become the most excellent mouth among my equals.
O Waters, you are immortality; make me immortal. May our slaves be many; may there be abundance of horses and cattle in me. May prosperity be mine. (Oṃ).
"Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ janad om"—with these words, he silently pours [the water] into himself, [saying]:
"Thou art splendor; thou art immortality."
With these words he touches his forehead.
Then he causes water to be brought, saying, "Water for sipping, sir.
Having sipped it with the *jīvā* verses, [he continues].
(KauśS_12,1[90].23) Then they announce the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) to him, saying, "The honey-mixture with two attendants;
'Yes'. (KauśS_12,1[90].24) With two branches below and one above, it is covered.
(KauśS_12,1[90].25) "The winds bring sweetness for the one who follows the cosmic order" (PS 19.45.5).
Thus, with these very [verses], there is the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*);
likewise, there is the response (*pratimantraṇa*):
"The winds blow sweetly for the one who follows the cosmic order; the rivers flow with sweetness."
May the cows be sweet for us.
Sweet be the night and sweet the dawn; sweet be the earthly realm;
may the plants be sweet for us.
May the Lord of the Forest be full of sweetness for us; may the Sun be full of sweetness;
may the Sky, our father, be full of sweetness.
With the words, "I gaze upon you with the eye of Sūrya," he gazes back.
Having received it with the formulas "I am united" and "Of the god Savitṛ," he places it facing eastward with its handle pointing east.
Having placed it on the ground with the words, "I set thee on the navel of the earth,
in the lap of Aditi," he moves it clockwise with two fingers, and taking hold of it with the ring finger and the thumb, he consumes it.
(“Oṃ bhūs tat savitur vareṇyaṃ bhūḥ svāhā,” thus the first;
“bhargo devasya dhīmahi bhuvaḥ svāhā.”)
"Thus the second.
(KauśS 12,2[91].8) "May he who shall impel our thoughts [svaḥ svāhā]"—
thus the third.
"May we meditate upon the god's [gift]; let him generate it, svāhā!"—this is the fourth [offering].
"The swift enjoyment of the god; let it increase, svāhā!"—[thus the fifth].
"Thus [the fifth] (KauśS 12,2[91].11);
'May he do [it], svāhā!'— thus the sixth."
"May it grow, svāhā!"— this is the seventh [offering].
"The great one, svāhā!"— [this is the eighth].
Thus is the eighth;
"That, svāhā! thus is the ninth.
(“*Śam svāhā*,” thus the tenth; “*Oṃ*,” thus the eleventh.)
(17) The twelfth [offering] is performed silently.
(18) Having eaten of that [food] as if it were a mere remnant, one should give it to a Brāhmaṇa who is learned in the Vedas.
(19) If such a learned Brāhmaṇa cannot be found, one should give it to a Śūdra.
Now, there is also this Vedic verse:
"O Brāhmaṇas, he drinks this Soma who eats whatever he may eat;
let him not give the remains of his food to one who is not a Brāhmaṇa. (KauśS 12.2[91].20)
"Let him who does not drink *soma* drink the *soma*," so it is said (*Lāṭyāyana Śrautasūtra* 2.12.17).
Curds and honey constitute the *madhuparka* for a Brāhmaṇa;
milk-rice (*pāyasa*) constitutes the *madhuparka* for an Indra-like guest (*aindra*).
Honey and clarified butter constitute the *madhuparka* for Soma;
a stirred drink (*mantha*) and clarified butter constitute the *madhuparka* for Pūṣan;
and milk and clarified butter constitute the *madhuparka* for Sarasvatī.

Surā and clarified butter constitute the *mausala* honey-mixture (*madhuparka*); indeed, this occurs in two [rites], namely the *sautrāmaṇī* and the *rājasūya*. Water and clarified butter constitute the *vāruṇa* honey-mixture.
(12.3.9) Oil and clarified butter are the *madhuparka* of Śrāvaṇa;
(12.3.10) oil and a rice-ball are the *madhuparka* of the wandering mendicant (*pārivrājaka*).
Thus, indeed, this *madhuparka* is of nine kinds.
(KauśS_12,3[92].12) Then they announce a cow to him, saying, "O, a cow! (KauśS_12,3[92].13) He addresses them with this mantra:
"Thou art being; thou art becoming; be food, be breath, be manifold."
He releases [the child] by means of the name "Jyeṣṭhā" [recited] by name: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svar janad oṃ.
[She is] the mother of the Ādityas, the daughter of the Vasus, the sister of the Rudras, the navel of immortality.
Proclaim this to the people who understand: do not slay the cow, the sinless Aditi!
"Oṃ, let the cow eat the grass," he says; with the words "From good pasture... he addresses her as she sets out.
The honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) is not red.
We do not recognize the formula "Give permission"; one should simply say, "Do it.
[With the words] "O axe, do not harm him" (*svadhite mainaṃ hiṃsīḥ*).
With the words, "Thus he offers the sacrificial weapon" (KauśS 12.3.19), he hands over the *śastra*;
with the words, "Drive away my evil" (KauśS 12.3.20), he addresses the performer;
they should prepare the omentum (*vapā*) dedicated to Agni.
Or rather, a Brāhmaṇa alone should consume it, for that oblation belongs to that deity. Then, for him, there is bathing, unguent, a garland, and ointment;
whatever is to be collected here, having collected that—
Then the attendants announce, "O sir, we are indeed attendants.
He addresses them in reply:
"May we be more numerous, and may those who are our superiors also become more numerous; and may others besides us also be born in greater numbers."
And [the priest] says, "Of this giver," looking toward the giver.
Then those who have obtained food and drink announce, "O, we have obtained food and drink! He addresses them with a mantra.
"May we be eaters of food, and may those who have made us non-eaters of food [be so no longer]; and may others also become our more abundant eaters of food.
(KauśS 12.3.29) With the words "and of this giver," he looks at the giver.
(KauśS 12.3.30) When the food has been brought, he offers an oblation.

With this verse, "O you who desire, desiring what [we offer], we prepare this oblation for you," [one should act]. (KauśS 12.3[92].31) [The verse begins: "O you who desire, desiring what, we prepare this oblation for you..."
"May all that be fulfilled for us; now, partake of this oblation, svāhā! (KauśS 12.3[92].32).

This is the ritual procedure for the teacher, this is the ritual procedure for the officiating priest, this is the ritual procedure for the associate, this is the ritual procedure for marriage, this is the ritual procedure for the guest—this is the ritual procedure for the guest.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter of the Kauśika-sūtra of the Atharvaveda. Now,
the portents.
In the rain,
among the yakṣas,
and in the mouth of a jackal.
In a family beset by strife, during an earthquake, or when there is an eclipse of the sun.
And [the rites] for the moon, at the rising of the dawn, at the conjunction,
and at the [lunar] eclipse.
When there is a suspicion of sorcery,
while Brāhmaṇas are bearing weapons,
and while the deities are dancing, leaping, laughing, and singing.
At the joining of the two ploughs,
at the joining of the ropes and the bodies [of the oxen], and at the contact with fire.
The oblation from a cow that has lost its calf, from a mare, from a she-ass, and from a human woman; wherever cows yield red milk.
(13.1.20) While the cow suckles at the bull; (13.1.21) while the cow suckles at the cow;
(13.1.22) in the foam of the sky.
When ants appear; when blue flies appear; when honey-bees appear.
In the unknown,
in the rent,
in the waterless, in the water-unfolding.
When the sesame seeds have become uniform in oil,
when the sacrificial oblations have been touched, and when the whirlpools turn counter-clockwise.
When it grows upon a sacrificial post,
when it is in a firebrand, or when it is in a comet, he fumigates the Seven Sages.
When the stars have fallen from their positions, when meat falls into the mouth,
and when there is a glow without fire—
When the fire hisses;
when the clarified butter, the oil, and the honey overflow;
and when the domestic fire burns down the hall.
When a new bamboo shoot sprouts, when a water-jar bursts, when the cooking pot cracks open, and when the grain for the parched flour swells.

Now, when these rains fall— rain consisting of clarified butter, meat, honey, gold, and whatever other terrible rains may fall— then that family, village, or district perishes. In such a case, the king, the lord of the earth, should seek out a learned Brahmin.
He who knows the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases is indeed wise. For these—the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases—are the pacifiers and protectors of all this.
He says: "Prepare [the materials]!"
They prepare for it a bronze vessel, two large garments, pure clarified butter, pacifying herbs, and a new water-pitcher.
There are three joints of the ritual: the full moon day, the new moon day, and an auspicious lunar mansion.
Even if it be at any other time, one may perform it for one who is afflicted.

Having bathed, wearing unwashed garments, fragrant, observing the vow, and fit for the ritual, he fasts for one night, three nights, six nights, or twelve nights. On the morning of the twelfth day, where that [object] has fallen, he kindles the fire from there on, sweeps around it, sprinkles water, spreads sacrificial grass (*barhis*), places a vessel of water nearby, and performs the service with clarified butter (*ājya*).
Having offered the regular oblations in front and the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*),
he then offers [the following]:
"The streams of clarified butter that rain down here, the cooked meat, the honey, and the gold— "
May these showers follow after my enemy; may the showers of water be abundant for me.
Whether it be a rain of blood, a rain of honey-dust, or whatever other terrible and undesirable rain there may be—let all these follow after the hater; let them turn back and depart away from him.
Having offered with "To Agni, svāhā," he should offer oblations with the names of the Mothers, beginning with "The divine Gandharva."
A Brāhmaṇa should give a choice ox to the performer; a Vaiśya, a plough; a local ruler, a horse; and a king, an excellent village. That is the expiation in that case.
Now, when these yakṣas are seen—namely, a monkey, a beast of prey, a crow, or a human form—it is to be regarded as a source of apprehension.
In that case, one should offer an oblation with [the verse]:
“If a monkey, a beast of prey, or a crow, O Jātavedas, should fall upon this kingdom; if a swift man-demon should fall [upon it]...”
May all these go after the hater; may they turn back and go away from him.
Having offered with "To Agni, svāhā," he should offer oblations with the names of the Mothers, beginning with "The divine Gandharva."
That is the expiation in that case.
Now, there are two frogs named Gomāyu; wherever they speak, thinking, "He is speaking toward me! He is speaking toward me!"—if one should have such a suspicion, one should offer an oblation there.
O Jātavedas, when the two jackals howl with discordant voices,
as if gnashing their teeth, let these two— the Rathantara and the Bṛhat Sāmans— roar against the one who hates us.
With the *rathantara* I pacify you through the *bṛhat*; with the *bṛhat* I pacify you through the *rathantara*.
Indra and Agni, increasing you through sacred prayer (*brahman*), shall make you long-lived and most excellent.
Having offered with the mantra, "To Indra and Agni, svāhā! (PS 1.83.4cd),
[he recites] "The divine Gandharva" (2.2.1).
Thus one should offer oblations with the names of the Mothers;
that is the expiation there.
Now, when a family becomes quarrelsome, they say that it is seized by Nirṛti.
Therein one should offer two oblations with the verse: "From afar [drive away] the enemy" (RV 8.2.12). And:
"O Agni, you are the *ayās* and free from reproach; truly, you are the *ayās*. (KauśS 13.5)
Made with an unwearied mind, you, being unwearied, have carried the oblation;
bestow healing medicine upon us.
Having offered into the fire with "Svāhā," one should offer these oblations in that very place:
"Driving away the flesh-eating fire from afar, I set up this enclosure for you so that you may live."
O Indra and Agni, increasing you with sacred prayer, may you two, possessing long life, make me most excellent.
Having offered with the mantra, "To Indra and Agni, svāhā! (KauśS 13.5), he recites, "Let Nirṛti depart... (PS 19.23.4ff).
With this hymn, one should offer oblations:
"Let Nirṛti depart; let nothing whatsoever remain here for her.
May she drive away her snares and her hundred and one deaths."
Those hundred and one snares of yours, O Death, intended for the slaying of mortal man— those we all ward off with the magic power of the sacrifice.
Let the one hundred and one deaths belonging to Nirṛti depart from here; may we ward them off, for we establish within ourselves both the breath and the light that dispels their darkness.
O Varuṇa, those hundred and those thousand great sacrificial bonds of yours that are spread out—
from those may Varuṇa, Soma, Indra, all the gods, and the Maruts of beautiful praise release us.

"The Brahman has risen, shining, the intermediate space and the sky; the two Brahmans have shaken off death by means of immortality. The Brahman is the overseer of good deeds, the direct witness; may the Brahman drive away from us defilement and darkness.
(PS 16.150.2) "A choice ox," and so on, is the same as before. (KauśS 13,5[97].9)
Now, wherever this earthquake occurs, there one should offer an oblation:
"The sky is immovable; the intermediate space is immovable; the earth and these quarters are immovable.
Immovable from obstruction and confinement, as one who is firm and victorious, I establish myself in the kingdom."
As the sun shines in the sky, as Mātariśvan clothes the atmosphere,
and as Agni has entered the earth, so may this Dhruva be unshakable and victorious.
As the god thunders and shines resplendent in heaven, as he sends down rain for one who desires rain,
and as the waters have entered the earth— even so may this Dhruva be steadfast, unshakable, and victorious.
Just as the rivers flow day and night without ceasing toward the ocean with their sediment,
so may all the people, being of one mind, come here without fail to my invocation.
May the goddess Earth, together with the deities, be firm, stable, and immovable for me.
May she drive away all evil from us and pierce through my enemies who hate me.
Having offered with "To the Earth, svāhā! (cf. AVPariś 11.1.11), he recites "I have brought thee hither" (RV 6.87.1) and "Firm is the sky" (RV 6.88.1).
One should offer oblations with this section beginning "Truth is great" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.1.1);
that is the expiation in that case.
Now, when darkness seizes the sun, one should offer an oblation there with [the verse]:
"Even the celestial, variegated one, ordaining the seasons, rises up, causing the fierce one to revolve among the seasons.
May that Āditya come forward, advancing from all sides; the waters move along these worlds."
In harmony with the medicinal herbs, may Indra and Agni protect you;
by means of the cosmic order and the word of truth, destroy all darkness.
Having offered with "To Āditya, svāhā! (KauśS 13.7[99].3),
one should sacrifice with this hymn beginning with "The overcomer, the conqueror" (RV 10.180.1).
He worships with red [animals];
that is the expiation in that case. Now, when the moon is eclipsed, one should offer oblations there.
Rāhu pursues King Svaran; he strikes him down here first.
A thousand of his bodies must perish here; let a hundred of his bodies be destroyed.
Having offered with "To Candra, svāhā," one should offer with this hymn: "The smoke of dung, the constellations... (RV 6.128.1).
That is the expiation in that case.
Now, where this Dawn does not rise, there one should offer [the oblation]:
"May the Fortune of the Dawn arise, fashioning [her work]; having made the straw-bundles ready, let the grey-haired wanderer go forth."
Bearing the seasons in their many diverse forms, she who knows all things ordains what is auspicious for me.
Having offered with "To the Dawn, svāhā," he should offer oblations with the names of the Mothers, beginning with "The divine Gandharva."
That is the expiation in that case.
Now, when the year becomes harsh, one should offer oblations there:
"The year that goes reddish-brown shakes off the offspring of Prajāpati."
We fashion you so that the deities may know that satisfaction.
We fashion you, O doe with a golden belly, the mother of the hunter.
We fashion you, such as you are.
"Whatever is your terrible [power], whatever is your poison—that we deposit among the enemies; [name the enemy]—so he should say.

(KauśS 13.10[102].3) Having offered the oblation with "With auspiciousness, with prosperity, with peace, with long life, for equality, svāhā! (KauśS 13.10[102].4), [he recites] "O Agni, may you be equal to us... (2.6.1).
One should offer oblations with this hymn;
that is the expiation in that case.
Now, wherever they suspect there are *upatārakas*, one should offer oblations there.
May the Revatīs—the bright, vigorous, and rejoicing ones—enter into the smoke of the skin.
Beyond that, may the waters enter into the earth; may the waters flow through these worlds.
Having offered with "To the waters, svāhā! (KauśS 13.11),
[he recites] "Let them fly up" (4.15.1) and "Burst forth" (7.18.1).
"One should offer the *varṣī* oblations;
that is the expiation for that occasion.
Now, one should offer them wherever the Brahmins are armed with weapons.
Those who are Asuras and humans, who carry bows and have human faces, moving here as spies—
we, though humans, enter into those gods as gods.
"May Indra be our leader; may he protect us on all sides.
Svāhā to Indra!"—having thus offered the oblation.
One should offer oblations with these two hymns: "May they not find us" (RV 1.19.1) and "Homage to the slayers of the gods" (RV 6.13.1).
That is the expiation in that case.
Now, when these deities dance, drip [with sweat], laugh, sing, or assume other forms—
whether they be asuras or humans— [one should act accordingly].
One should offer oblations with those [mantras] that provide protection from fear, namely: *mā no vidan* [1.19.1], *namo devavadhebhyaḥ* [6.13.1], and so forth.
That is the expiation in that case.
Now, when they are thus mingling at the plough, having cooked a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) and having gone halfway into the forest—
Having established the furrow facing east,
having placed the fuel-stick facing east in the middle of the furrow,
having swept around it, sprinkled water around it, and strewn sacrificial grass around it, he should set up the *śamyā* markers as enclosing sticks.
Then he offers the oblation:
"Thou art acquisition, thou art prosperity, thou art fortune; belonging to the descendants of Prajāpati, thee, desiring prosperity, I offer upon myself, svāhā!
"The lotus-laden pond, the furrow, beautiful in every limb."
Agriculture has been established in a thousand ways; this prosperity rests within me.
Men call you the wide earth; they know you as the glory of the mind. Bestow upon us a store of food that is free from disease and full of vigor.
[—, cf. ŚāṅkhGS 1.27.7, etc.
O wife of Parjanya, you who are golden and victorious, speak for us;
O you with black eyes, enjoy our oblation and grant satisfaction to our bipeds and quadrupeds.

With those [powers] by which the gods fashioned the Asuras, the Yātus, the Manus, the Gandharvas, and the Rākṣasas— with those, O auspicious one, come to us today with a gracious mind, bestowing thousandfold prosperity.
[— cf. 7.48.2cd] (The lotus-pond with its golden garland, dark-hued and beautiful in every limb, the furrow with its golden border—may this Śrī be established within me.)

O Goddess, being in harmony with the Aśvins, with Indra, with bounty, and with prosperity, come to us! May all the people and the quarters accord to you; may days and nights, half-months, months, and the seasonal periods together with the seasons grant you favor.
The supporter of gods and mortals, the supporter of offspring and of men;
together with elephants, other mounts, field-guardians, and charioteers—
with gold, horses, and cattle— may this Fortune (Śrī) be established in me.
At this point, one should employ the *śūnāsīra* rites;
[the offering of] a choice ox is the same as before.
Now, when two women, either spinning or weaving, join their threads together...
One should offer oblations with this hymn, beginning with "For Manā, the first thread... (PS 2.87.1):
"Manā beheld the first thread; others wove it out. (KauśS 13.15[107].2) [Manā beheld the first thread; others wove it out.]
Therefore I speak to you, O women: may you be virtuous and may you be fertile.
May your thread be successful; may the chosen chariot proceed successfully.
And so, O swift ones, run forth at dawn to draw [the chariot].
Like swift screech-owls, like the fierce descent of waters,
let them fly down like swift birds upon the fertile fields by the straight path.
Your two hindquarters throb as if with the pricking of two mules;
I have now proclaimed the hymn of the fertile fields that lie in wait.
"A woman weaves the fifth ray as a garment of wealth; may he be uninjured while wearing it. O Indra, put on the garment and spread it out. One should give the garment to the maker.
That is the expiation in that case.
Now, when fire is thus mixed with fire [with the mantra]:
"May you two be of one mind and one dwelling for us."
With this hymn one should offer oblations:
"May you two be of one mind with us, sharing the same dwelling, and free from blemish.
Do not harm the lord of the sacrifice nor the sacrifice itself, O Jātavedas; be auspicious to us today. (cf. VSM 5.3, etc. (KauśS 13.16[108].2)
Agni is united with Agni, the sage, the youthful Bṛhaspati,
the bearer of oblations whose mouth is the sacrificial ladle.
"For you, O Agni, by means of fire; being a sage through a sage, a true one through a true one, a friend through a friend, are kindled."
(See RV 8.43.14) Protect us, O Agni, with one [hymn], protect us also with a second;
protect us with three songs, O Lord of Strength, protect us with four, O Vasu!
"May Samīcī and Mahanī protect me; may I not sit upon the long-lived Ṛc.
As a protector of my body, may I move through the world that finds wealth, following the Sāman.
(PS 20.52.4–5) One should give a gold ornament to the performer.
That is the expiation in that case. Now, when he produces twin boys, having sprinkled her with water for pacification and caused her to be milked,
one should cook a *sthālīpāka* in the milk of that very cow.
Having placed the fuel-wood towards the east,
having swept around, having sprinkled water, having strewn the sacrificial grass, and having set down a vessel of water, [he recites:
"By each single creation he came into being" (RV 3.28.1).
Offering clarified butter with this hymn,
he pours the remnants into a water-vessel; he pours the final remnant back into the cooked rice.
Then he causes the cow and the two calves to eat; he causes them to sip water from a vessel of water and sprinkles them.
He should give that [cow] to him alone.
That is the expiation in this case.
Now, if it should be a mare or a she-donkey, having placed the fuel-wood toward the east in this very manner,
having strewn [the grass] in this very manner,
and having set down [the offerings] in this very manner—
Offering clarified butter with this very hymn,
he pours the remnants into a water-vessel;
from that water-vessel, he causes them to sip water and sprinkles them.
One should give that very [cow] to him;
that is the expiation in that case.
Now, if it should be a human [sacrifice], one should likewise pile the fuel-wood towards the east.
Having strewn [the grass] in this manner,
having placed [the offerings] in this manner,
and having placed the two newborn infants upon his lap;
Offering clarified butter with this very hymn,
he pours the residues of the oblations (*saṃpātān*) in succession upon their heads, beginning with the verse "I [place] him upon the head of his mother" for the two sons;
the subsequent residues he pours into a water-vessel.
He causes them to sip water from a vessel of water and sprinkles them;
he should give that [vessel] to him alone;
that is the expiation in this case.
Its ransom is according to its worth or according to what is available.
Now, regarding that place where cows yield red milk:
"He who anoints himself with human flesh" (TS 8.3.15).
With these four [verses] one should offer oblations;
one should give a choice cow to the performer;
that is the expiation in this case.
Now, where the bull suckles the cow, there one should sacrifice with [the verse]:
"The bull sucked the cow; Indra entered the form of a cow.
Grant us prosperity, nourishment, and long life."
Having offered with "To Indra, svāhā! (KauśS 13.21),
[he recites] "May they not find us" (1.19.1) and "Homage to the slayers of the gods" (6.13.1).
With these two hymns one should offer oblations;
that is the expiation there. Now, where a cow sucks another cow, there one should offer oblations.
(The cow who provides security and prosperity, the consort of the prize, has been sent forth by Indra and Agni while they yawn;
therefore, O Agni, protect me from that which is terrible. May our couples be born forth according to their forms.)
Having offered with "To Indra and Agni, svāhā! (cf. KauśS 128.2), [he recites] "The divine Gandharva... (KauśS 13.22[114].3; 2.2.1).
Thus one should offer oblations with the names of the Mothers;
that is the expiation for that.
Now, wherever a cow, a horse, a mule, or a human smells the foam from the sky, there one should offer oblations.
Milk among the gods, milk among the plants, milk in the quarters, milk in the intermediate space—may Dhātṛ and Savitṛ bestow that upon me; may all the gods together proclaim it.
The milk that is in the waters, the milk in the cows, the milk in the wells and in the mountains—may Dhātṛ and Savitṛ bestow that upon me; may all the gods together approve it.
Whatever milk is present in wild animals, whatever moves and flies among the winged birds—may Dhātṛ and Savitṛ bestow that upon me; may all the gods together praise it.
The waters that have been bestowed from heaven, and those many which exist in various ways in the intermediate space—
of them, O ruling and sovereign Heaven and Earth, grant us a portion today, being free from anger.
One should offer oblations with this hymn [PS 1.91];
that is the expiation there.
Now, wherever ants of improper appearance are seen, one should offer oblations there.
(Svāhā to Bhuvā, svāhā to Bhuvana, svāhā to the Lord of Bhuvana, svāhā to the Lord of beings, svāhā to Avoṣa, svāhā to Vinata, svāhā to Śatāruṇa.
(Svāhā to him who is the king of white ants in the eastern direction;
svāhā to him who is the king of black ants in the southern direction.)
To him who is the king of the silver ants in the western direction, svāhā!
To him who is the king of the red ants in the northern direction, svāhā!
To him who is the king of the brown ants in the fixed (zenith) direction, svāhā!
"To him who is the king of the green ants in the intermediate direction, svāhā!
To him who is the king of the reddish-brown ants in the upward direction, svāhā! (KauśS 13.24 [116].4).
If they should not be appeased by this much, then one should add fuel to the fire and proceed further.

Having strewn sacrificial grass made of *śara* reeds, cut on both ends, in a counter-clockwise direction (*prasavya*), he offers oblations with a *sruva*-ladle shaped like a *bādhaka* bird, using clarified butter that has been strained through a leaf of the *śāka* plant and mixed with *iṅguda* resin, while reciting:
"Arise! Run away! Let there be no more for you here! (KauśS 13.24). This is the *añcana* rite.
"Indra shall simultaneously split the embryos and the eggs of you all" (PS 17.13.3).
"Phaṭ! Strike the ants! (cf. KauśS 47.21)—thus (KauśS 13.24[116].8).
"Indra is yours, Yama is yours, Varuṇa is yours, Agni is yours, Vāyu is yours, Sūrya is yours, and Indra is yours, Prajāpati is yours, Īśāna is yours. Thus.
Now, where these blue flies of ill-omened appearance are seen, there one should offer an oblation:
"The terrible messengers of Death who travel in the same chariot with mortals have become flesh-eaters.
May the eye of the auspicious ones be auspicious, and may their cry be auspicious; may it be well for our bipeds and well for our quadrupeds."
Peaceful is the eye of the crows, as is that terrible emission of their minds.
O Lord of the Mind, protect me with your body from what is terrible; do not harm me in my body, nor in my offspring, nor in my cattle. To Vāyu, svāhā!
Having offered this oblation with the verse, "May Vāta breathe forth the medicine... (PS 19.46.7, etc.).
With this hymn one should offer oblations:
"May Vāta blow healing upon us, bringing auspiciousness and joy to our heart;
may he prolong our lives."
And you, O Vāta, are our father, and you are our brother and our friend;
as such, grant us life.
"O Vāta, that medicine which is placed in your house, hidden in secret— that give us for the sake of living. With this hymn, one should offer oblations.
That is the expiation in that case.
Now, when honey-bees of improper appearance are seen, [one should recite]:
"The winds blow honey for the one who follows the cosmic order" (*madhu vātā ṛtāyate*). *Pariśiṣṭa* 19.45.5.
One should offer oblations with this hymn (cf. KauśS 90.25–91.1);
that is the expiation for that occasion.
Now, wherever this unknown portent is seen, there one should offer oblations.
Whatever is unknown, unrecited, or mutually inconsistent regarding the purpose or the ritual act— O Agni, protect us from that, for you indeed know each thing as it truly is.
"To Agni, svāhā!"—and also "O Vāyu, Sūrya, Candra!"—thus [it is said].
"The purpose of the rite is commensurate with man; the purpose of the action is commensurate with man."
May Vāyu protect me from that, for he indeed knows each thing as it truly is.
"Vāyave svāhā," and "Agnir mā, sūryo mā, candro mā," and so forth.
Now, if this [vessel] should break in a village, in a settlement, in a fire-sanctuary, or at a sacrificial assembly, four cows are prepared: a white one, a black one, and a ruddy one.
The fourth [cow] is Surūpā.
One sets aside the butter produced from the milk of these [cows] over a period of twelve nights.
On the morning of the twelfth day, having added fuel to the fire at the very spot where it previously burst open, [one proceeds].
Having swept around, sprinkled water around, and strewn sacrificial grass (barhis) around, and having mixed the ghee from a white cow,
he consecrates it with the three verses beginning with "Agni on the earth" (AVŚ 12.1.19), and then touches it.
Then he should offer oblations:
likewise in the southern half,
likewise in the western half.
Having placed [the offering] in the northern half, one should offer oblations with the Vāstoṣpati hymns.
Having brought the remnants of the offerings into the cracked [vessel] and having completed the oblations,
one should sprinkle the cracked [vessel] with water for pacification.
A Brāhmaṇa should give those very [gifts]; a Vaiśya, a plow; a local ruler, a horse; and a king, an excellent village. That is the expiation in that case.
Now, when this place becomes flooded with water despite being waterless,
one should offer oblations with the hymns addressed to the waters (*apsu-sūkta*), beginning with "Golden-hued" (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*).
That is the expiation in that case. Now, where sesame seeds become mixed with oil, there one should offer oblations:
"To the non-deficient, svāhā!"
Svāhā to the imperishable! Svāhā to the immeasurable!
Svāhā to the perfectly complete!
If he should hate someone, he should pour [the blood] toward that person's direction while facing south, saying: "I sprinkle this blood upon you."
Now, when they should encounter birds, or bipeds and quadrupeds, having touched either the omentum or the sacrificial oblations, [they recite]:
"The fires that...
and "Homage to those who strike down the gods."
One should offer oblations with these two hymns;
that is the expiation for that occasion.
Now, wherever there are two whorls on the head of a boy or a girl—one turning to the left and one being a localized whorl—one should offer an oblation there.
Tvaṣṭṛ, who transforms forms in many ways and brings forth offspring of manifold appearances, may he fashion us without error; may he arrange us here in this very place, one after another.
To Tvaṣṭṛ, svāhā!
He weaves in many ways within the wombs, generating offspring of manifold forms;
may he make it right for me, and may he fashion us here in due order.
To Tvaṣṭṛ, svāhā!
Whether it has been wiped away or not wiped away, whether they wipe it crosswise or otherwise— may the god Savitṛ make that auspicious, and Prajāpati, in harmony with his creatures.

To Tvaṣṭṛ, svāhā! O God, may those joints of yours which turn to the left, those that are multiform, and those that turn backward— may they be many, manifold, pleasant, efficacious, and auspicious for him.
Having offered with the formula "To Tvaṣṭṛ, svāhā!
(KauśS 13.32), one should sacrifice with this hymn: "May Tvaṣṭṛ [accept] my divine speech" (RV 6.4.1).
That is the expiation in that case.
Now, where this sacrificial post sprouts, there one should offer an oblation with [the verse]:
"The sacrificial post, sprouting with a hundred branches, the sacrifice itself, encompassing and seeking to delude the worlds of the sacrificer..."
Guarded by the Vedas, surrounded by Brahmā, and pacified by the Atharvans, may it go to the worlds of those who have performed good deeds.
The sacrificial post has indeed ascended for the slaying of enemies; may neither my sacrifice nor the sacrificer suffer harm.
Place this sacrifice and the sacrificer in that world where the Seven Seers of good deeds dwell.
Having offered with the mantra, "O Lord of the Forest, svāhā! (cf. KātyŚS 2.2.8), he recites:
"The Lord of the Forest has come to us together with the gods" (RV 10.3.15).
Thus one should offer oblations;
that is the expiation for that occasion.
Now, when a meteor falls from the sky at such a time, it portends a threat to security and well-being, or a threat of drought.
In that regard, the king, the lord of the earth, should choose a learned Brahmin as his priest (*brahmán*).
Having been chosen, he should go halfway into the forest and fast there for twelve nights.
For the first nine nights, he should subsist on wild vegetables, roots, and fruits; then, for the final three nights, he should consume nothing other than water.
On the following day, seven milch-cows are prepared: a white one, a black one, a ruddy one, a blue one, a pale-red one, a well-formed one, and a multiformed one as the seventh.
One sets aside the butter produced from the milk of these cows, which has been collected over the course of twelve nights.
On the morning of the twelfth night, having established the fire to the north of the very spot where that [butter] fell, one proceeds.
Having swept around, sprinkled water around, and strewn sacrificial grass (*barhis*) around,
he then melts butter in a golden vessel and, with a golden dipping-spoon (*sruva*), offers it with hymns that slay demons,
beginning with: "Her they call Tārakā, the long-haired one" (AV 5.17.4).
Offering clarified butter with this hymn (*sūkta*),
having brought together the remnants of the oblations (*saṃpāta*) when [the fire] has fallen out, and having completed the offerings,
he sprinkles the fallen [fire] with water for pacification (*śāntyudaka*).
A Brāhmaṇa should give those very [gifts]; a Vaiśya, a plow; a local ruler, a horse; and a king, an excellent village. That is the expiation in that case.
(KauśS_13,35[127].1) Now, when this comet (dhūmaketu) scorches the Seven Sages (saptarṣi), it is said that there is a danger to security and well-being (ayogakṣema).

(KauśS_13,35[127].2) Five animals are sacrificed: a black bull for Varuṇa; a goat, a horse, a ram, or a tawny-colored one for Vāyu; a multicolored one for the Quarters (diśya); a ewe for the Maruts; one for Agni; and one for Prajāpati;
as well as milk-rice for Apāṃ Napāt, and a porpoise.
Having praised Varuṇa three times with the verse, "And this earth... (KauśS 13.35[127].3), he recites, "In the waters, O King... (KauśS 13.35[127].4).
Thus one should offer four oblations for Varuṇa with [the verse]:
"O Vāyu, capture the deer for us who are hunting; bring them to us most closely, for the wind is made of reins" (PS 20.51.4).
Thus for the rite pertaining to Vāyu; "Of the quarters" for the rite pertaining to the directions.
"To that beautiful sacrifice,
you are summoned for protection; O Agni, come with the Maruts"—
this is for the offering to the Maruts.
"Fire from the waters"—
this is for the verse addressed to Agni;
"Prajāpati from the ocean"— this is for the verse addressed to Prajāpati.
With these verses addressed to Prajāpati (KauśS 13,35[127].10), one should cause the water-jar to enter the waters together with the hymns of the waters and a piece of gold (KauśS 13,35[127].11);
then it will surely rain.
In that case, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of one's entire property;
its ransom may be according to what is appropriate or according to what is available.
Then, at the time when the stars appear as if they are falling down, one should offer the oblation there.
O Jātavedas, whatever constellation falls before King Soma with impetuous force, from that terrible one, O Agni, protect me; may our offspring be born in pairs according to their forms.
Having offered with "To Indra and Agni, svāhā! (cf. KauśS 114.2), [he recites] "King Soma and King Savitṛ... (PS 19.33.1).
One should offer oblations with this hymn:
"King Soma and King Savitṛ, King Bhūvas and King Bhuvana, King Śarva and King Śarma— may those gods grant us protection."
May Bṛhaspati with the Ādityas, and Bhaga together with Soma,
and all the gods in the wide mid-air— may those gods grant us protection.
"And whether ignorant or knowing, go away with your head severed, like a blood-drinking [weapon], each according to its proper place.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter of the Kauśikasūtra in the Atharvaveda. One should occupy the sacrificial site according to its layout;

Studying one quarter [of the Veda] in the first watch of the night, one quarter in the last watch, and sleeping during the middle watch;

When the ritual materials have been collected, both the Brahman priest and the king, having bathed, wearing unwashed garments, fragrant, observing their vows, and fit for the rite, fast.

Day by day his kingdom becomes greater; he becomes the sole king upon this earth; he does not die before old age—this is true for him who knows thus, and for him who, knowing thus, performs the *indramaha* sacrifice.
Now we shall explain the rule for the study of the Veda.
Having performed the *upākaraṇa* ceremony on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada, they should study for four and a half months; in this manner [they study] the Vedic meters (*chandas*),
and there is no cutting off of hair.
(And having performed the *upākaraṇa*, they should spend half a month [studying], after releasing [the study] for three days.
The commencement is said to be on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa; the release is said to be on the full moon of Pauṣa.
Now we shall declare the occasions when study is forbidden (*anadhyāya*).
In the *brahmajya* sacrifice, [the ritual] is suspended;
in the *śrāddha*, at the rising from birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), and in vomiting— these three require the performance of the *caraṇa*.
When the teacher has died, or in the case of those whose birth is human,
one should act toward them exactly as toward those for whom a *śrāddha* is performed.
Having accepted all the substances intended for a *śrāddha*, provided they have not been kept for more than ten days, there shall be a suspension of Vedic study (*anadhyāya*).
(Regarding) animate and inanimate objects for the purpose of cleaning the teeth,
and in the case of contact with a razor.
When the fires have been kindled,
at midnight when lightning flashes and thunder rolls, [one should offer] seven times; when the rain has ceased until morning, [one should offer] up to the time of the morning meal.
In the event of rain, a thunderclap, or an earthquake.
Accompanied by light, even during the season, until the time [of the event];
there is no engagement on uneven ground.
Now we shall state the measurement; it is the same as that for lightning and meteors.
In the dark fortnights of the months of Mārgaśīrṣa, Pauṣa, and Māgha, there are three Aṣṭakās;
on the new moon day as well,
there are three occasions for the suspension of Vedic study.
(At birth and at death, a period of ten nights is prescribed;
for a teacher, it shall be ten nights, as well as for all those of one's own kin.
At a birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), however, one should not study for a single day; one should avoid the sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*) for three nights.

One should avoid the wife of the teacher’s son, as well as a student who has studied together with him, a subordinate teacher, and one who has approached for instruction, for a day and a night; likewise, one should avoid a fellow celibate student and a king.
(Regarding the portents occurring outside their proper season: All portents such as thunderclaps and the like are traditionally held to be [inauspicious] regardless of the specific season;
and whatever other divine marvels there may be, they should all be treated like thunderclaps.

(Regarding the *chāndasa* period of study during the proper season, it is traditionally prescribed as lasting until the end of the rainy season; any time after the morning meal during the proper season that constitutes a suspension of study reaches the evening twilight.)
The entire evening [of study] is suspended; when lightning flashes at night during the *nigada* [period], one should not recite the remainder [of the lesson].
When the sun has set, there is proficiency [in recitation] after two or three [such] occurrences.
Then, having eaten for that much time, at nightfall and during both twilights—

If they study during the months of Pauṣa or Āṣāḍha when clouds appear,
and rain, lightning, or thunder occurs,
they should observe a three-night fast, remaining standing or sitting, practicing celibacy, and consuming tasteless food.
